title: [Kill Team] Tactical Focus: Deployment 101
content:
It’s easy to overlook deployment in almost any tabletop game. I doubt that anyone is eagerly bounding over to a table because they simply cannot wait to take their dudes out of a case and place them on a board in the just right formation. Folks play tabletop wargames for the battles, the pretend war, the tiny plastic glory to be earned by rolling dice and pushing models around a board. For many players, especially those just starting out, deployment is just the act of setting up for the good stuff to follow.

Deployment isn’t the sexiest part of a game in any system, but an early lesson that most people learn early on is that no matter the system, deployment is one of the most important parts of any game. While good deployment rarely can win you a game all on its own, bad deployment can absolutely lose you a game before the very first turn. The key to winning any game is making sure your models are where they need to be on the board, when they need to be there, and poor deployment makes it all that much harder for you to do that. Poor deployment means you’ll waste time getting your forces to where they actually need to be on the board, all while key moments that you could’ve taken advantage of slip through your fingers.

Credit: Games Workshop

Kill Team is no different then any of these systems, and in some cases good deployment versus bad deployment can be even more pivotal than in many larger games since you have a much smaller number of models on the board to cover space. The last thing you want to realize in the middle of a match is that your operative with the nasty gun ended up somewhere on the board where they’ll never get the chance to shoot at a good target because they were deployed badly, and you didn’t figure it out until it’s too late.

So what are the best practices for good deployment in Kill Team? In this article, we’ll take a dive into a four step thought process behind building a strong and consistent plan for deploying your team on the table to help you better understand and improve your gameplan, and set yourself up to win in the Killzone before the first round even starts.

Necron Canoptek Circle Kill Team. Credit: Magos Sockbert

Step One: Know Your Team

In theory, Kill Team is a game with a limited number of variables for building a deployment plan. Especially if using the Approved Ops ruleset, there’s only so many maps to play on, and only so many teams you could expect to play against. You could, given enough time, patience, and practice, learn each and every matchup and map and build a tailor made plan for each combination. In practice, that’s a huge number of potential matchups, which doubles in size when you realize you factor in that your plan might change depending on which side of the killzone you’re deploying on, and then multiply that further when you take into consideration the different crit ops and tac ops. While some players can plan for each and every possibility, for most it’s impractical to plan for each individually. While there are a few important things to think about for the opponents team, such as considering their most dangerous operatives and their team’s threat ranges, the most important part of deployment is understanding your own team's rules, and having a general game plan before deployment even starts.

Knowing your own rules is important to winning sounds like I’m stating the obvious, but just because it’s low hanging fruit doesn’t make it any less true. There’s a pretty substantial number of teams in the game, even with declassified rotating out older teams from competitive play, and it’s almost a guarantee that most players won’t remember every single rule for teams they don’t regularly play as or against. You, on the other hand, are a fixed variable: you know exactly what team you’re going to be playing, you control that. So, learn your team’s rules, look it over and learn what the team is good at and bad at. If you know your teams rules like the back of your hand, then thats quite literally half the battle of knowing what the teams on the killzone do.

Plus, once you know your rules, you can understand what your team is good at, and from there you can start to build a plan on how to win. Is your team tough and good at bullying enemy operatives off objectives? Do you play your Tac Ops extremely well? Are you an all gas no brakes Kill Op team? How's your mobility? What offensive tricks do you have? Can you swarm your opponent with bodies, or are you an elite team who needs to be more careful with each operative? While it is true that no plan survives first contact fully intact, it’s important to have a general idea of what your path to victory in a game will look like, as well as maybe a handful of alternate plans in case you end up with a matchup that makes plan A difficult to do.

If you feel comfortable and confident in your own knowledge, and have a solid basic gameplan, it hugely reduces the mental load during both deployment and the game in general. You can worry more about how your plan is changing as the game goes on, rather than trying to decide what the plan is on the fly, which is a huge relief from the mental load during a game. Plus, generally these kinds of plans that are prepared for pre-game are much more difficult for an opponent to stop than something improvised haphazardly, even if that pregame plan is fairly loose.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

Let’s take Murderwing, a team I’ve been playing extensively recently, as an example. I know that while this team has operatives that hit like a runaway freight train, it also has very limited defensive options and can lose operatives quickly if they’re hung out to dry, so generally I want to avoid just full sending the team unless I’m certain I can just overwhelm my opponent in a wall of Chaos Space Marine muscle. Because Murderwing is so mobile though, and I have great access to stuns and modifying APL, Murderwing can play the Crit Op and Tac Op fairly well, and thanks to Boost the team is super mobile and I can afford to hang back from objectives until I can zoom up and contest it safely. With this in mind, my general gameplan is to focus on Tac Op as my primary with Retrieval from Approved Ops 2025, and then focus on two objectives that I can stage safely far away from until I can fly up and take them near the end of a turning point. As a kicker, I can even send one operative on a long bomb run to the opponent home objective if I can get the right angle, which makes leaning on Retrieval even better. If I don’t think retrieval is going to work, I can pivot to Flank and use boost to reach safe spots in my opponents territory while picking off anyone sent my way, or Dominate if I can just get away with raking up kills in the back half of a game.

So without even seeing what map I’m playing on, or what team I’m up against, I’ve got the foundations of a gameplan and a path to how I will win. I’ll need to adjust for the unexpected of course, and there will always be the unexpected, but now when it's time to deploy I have a much better idea of where I need to place operatives so that they can be where they need to to execute the plan.

Step Two: Understand the Killzone

The next step in leveling up your deployment game is by understanding the various killzone maps in Kill Team, particularly in the Approved Ops mission pack.

While every Killzone will present a different set of problems and opportunities for your team, such as whether it’s open or close quarters and what sort of terrain and cover is nearby your drop zone, the main thing we’re going to focus on is what makes them all the same, and that’s how each Killzone can functionally be divided into three lanes based on where the objectives are placed on the map. Generally, if you take a look at any given Killzone and then split it into thirds based on where the objectives are placed, extending from drop zone to drop zone, these lanes become pretty easy to parse visually, even if they aren’t officially marked off from one another in any way.

While moving in between these three lanes can be very fluid in most games of Kill Team, during deployment it's important to decide how much you want to or need to control each of these lanes and deploy accordingly. Deciding to focus your efforts on controlling certain lanes tends to be a much more effective strategy than trying to spread your team out to be everywhere on the board at once, as it prevents you from being spread too thin and feeds back into your general game plan that you make prior to the start of the game.

As an example, if you know that you’re playing a team that wants to push aggressively into enemy territory, such as Vespid, it might be best to focus your deployment on the lane containing your opponents objective, where you’re likely to deliver the most pressure, while a smaller contingent of your forces hold the center and home objective lanes. For a team that wants to lie in wait, like Nemesis Claw, it may be best to ignore your opponent’s objective lane altogether and split your team between your home and center. While how your allocate your forces between each map may change based on the layout, understanding how to best split your team during deployment based on these three lanes will almost always be better than haphazardly trying to cover the whole board.

Step Three: Deploy Effective Equipment

Kill Team Volkus Terrain painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

One of the most unique aspects of Kill Team is equipment selection and how it can shape your team by providing a wide toolbox of options for every team to draw upon that can change from game to game. While there's a good bit of equipment that doesn’t affect deployment choices at all, many pieces of equipment, such as barricades, mines, and razorwire, can be deployed on the killzone prior to the start of the game. In many cases, effective deployment of equipment can be just as important as effective deployment of your operatives.

When boiled down to its most basic functions, deployable equipment generally has one of two purposes (though some pieces can be used for either option): The equipment either protects or aids your operatives, or the equipment denies or debuffs your opponent. Based on what you need each equipment piece to do, you’ll need to consider the placement of each piece differently, but either way you’ll once again want to think about killzone lanes.

Buffing or aiding your team can come in several different forms, such as a barricade to protect your models from shooting, a ladder to help get your model traverse vantage quickly, a comms device to boost support abilities, or an ammo cache to buff your shooting reliability. Deciding where these equipment choices need to go is usually pretty easy, as it largely depends on where you want your operatives to be. While that does again seem like a very silly and obvious statement to make, considering which lanes you want your team to focus on controlling during a game and deploying buff equipment in these areas means you’ll make the most out of where you place items like a comms device, or get the most protection out of a barricade. It's also important to think about how you want to stage up the board for later turning points with these equipment options, making it easier to project threat in parts of the killzone you want to control while making it difficult for the opponent to threaten you.

As an example, a barricade placed right on the center objective is strong, especially if it’s out in the open against shooting, but it might be so far forward that making the best use of it puts you in easy threat range of enemy operatives. Placing a barricade further back from the objective while keeping it in your operatives effective threat range, whether it’s shooting or charging, means that if your opponent wants to control the center objective, they have to walk within your threat range, and now you’re the one who can effectively start a trade from a safe staging position.  Consider what lanes and objectives you want to control, and how these choices will help improve your control over that part of the board.

The other function of deployable equipment can be trickier, but just as effective, and that's using deployable terrain as area denial. Deployable equipment used as denial pieces strengthens your control over a given lane by making it more difficult for your opponent to access it freely, slowing them down or corralling them into specific areas of the map. Examples of universal equipment choices that can do this include mines, razorwire, and even barricades placed at choke points that your enemy has to spend movement trying to climb. As far as where this denial equipment is usually most effective, they tend to be most effective in spots that either deny access to your home objective, or at choke points between lanes that make it difficult for your opponent to move freely from one lane to another should they have to redirect their forces. If there’s a part of the map you know you don’t want your opponent to be, and think your opponent will be able to easily get there if left unchecked, consider using deployable equipment options at those spots to slow down or deny your opponent access altogether.

Brood Brothers Kill Team. Credit: John from Can You Roll A Crit?

Step Four: Deploy Effective Operatives

A little over two thousand words later, and we’re finally on how we can best deploy our operatives.

After all of the considerations we’ve made so far, actually getting down to deploying our operatives might just be the easiest part here, since every decision we’ve made so far has set us up for success. We know what our path to winning the game looks like, we know what areas of the killzone we need to control to do it are, and we’ve set up our equipment to either improve our strength in a lane or deny the opponent free access. Every choice here has brought us to a razor sharp point that shows exactly where we need to be, which means when we’re deploying our team, we’re not just improvising or putting down operatives wherever. We can be purposeful in our decision, and maximize the effectiveness of our team.

The most important part of deployment, plan or no plan though, is to place your operatives in safe parts of your drop zone. This takes priority over all else, even if it means splitting your forces up more than you may like. An operative is no good to you if your opponent can grab an easy shot on it. If your safe spots are truly dire, consider using equipment to buy you more safe real estate in your drop zone.

Feral Mechanicum Kill Team; Credit: Colin Ward

Being purposeful is the key aspect here, and even if we’ve set up for success already, we still need to think on a per operative basis on where they will be most effective. For example, if you have an operative with a key support ability that improves your team’s offensive or defensive capabilities, they need to be deployed where you expect the bulk of your team to be, which means that this operative probably isn’t one you want babysitting your home objective. Or if you have a very aggressive operative, they need to be placed somewhere where you plan on the bulk of the engagement to be, as the last thing you want is to waste precious time trying to redeploy them because they were deployed too far away from the action.

Lastly, a good rule of thumb for deployment is think about where you want your models to be at the end of turning point one, and then set your model up in a spot where they can reach that part of the killzone when they activate. In the current edition of Kill team, turning point one doesn’t present any ability for your team to score outside of kill op, which almost always requires you to overextend your model, so that first turning point move is almost like a secondary deployment for the following three turning points. Just like with deployment, rather than just pushing your operatives directly up the board absentmindedly on the first turn, consider where you need to be to score points according to your game plan, and reposition your operatives in a spot to do so, even if it means potentially having a model not leave the drop zone so that it can be more effective later in the game. No matter where the operative needs to go that first turn though, the only way they can reach it is if they’re deployed in the right spot.

Credit: Dan "Swiftblade" Richardson

Final Thoughts

Deployment is the least interactive part of Kill Team, and while your opponents placement may influence your own placement of operatives and equipment, there's no randomness from the dice involved in deployment and no conflict to consider. It is entirely an operation that you, the player, control, and because of that it's one of the most important parts of the game to have a plan for. As stated earlier in the article, while deployment is something that very rarely wins a game all on its own, you can absolutely lose a game by deploying poorly before any dice are ever rolled. Deployment is the foundation for the rest of your game to follow, and with a carefully considered plan to build from and by deciding what lanes of the Killzone you need to focus your efforts on, it's much easier to set your equipment and operatives in positions to execute that strategy effectively and set yourself up to be in the strongest position possible for the rest of the match.

title: Legendary Warhammer sculptor Aly Morrison has died
content:
Influential Warhammer sculptor Aly Morrison has died; the announcement of his death was first made by specialist art trader Warhammer Original Artwork, and confirmed by Morrison's ex-wife Trish Carden, on Thursday October 12. Morrison's involvement in the early design of Warhammer and Warhammer 40,000 miniatures had a major impact on the development of the hobby and the Citadel aesthetic.

Morrison's career in miniature design began as a young man some time around 1977. Morrison contributed art to the Scottish D&D fanzine Underworld Oracle, and with the 'zine's co-editor Lou Nesbit developed models for the small Oracle Miniatures range. Morrison worked freelance for several companies including the historical miniature maker Mike's Models before coming to the attention of Bryan Ansell at Games Workshop, where he landed freelance work designing figures for Citadel Miniatures in 1983.

Long-time Warhammer fans may know Aly as part of a duo, Trish and Aly Morrison: today Trish is Trish Carden. They met in Edinburgh through mutual friend Donald Brotchie, who was studying jewellery and silversmithing with Trish at Edinburgh College of Art. Trish was fascinated by the detail Aly put into his miniatures and began to experiment with the medium. When Aly showed her work to Bryan Ansell she was also offered a job, creating the Citadel Studio's first (and likely only) power couple.

Aly and Trish married in 1984 and lived in a tiny top-floor tenement flat in Endinburgh for eighteen months, receiving orders from the Citadel studio and sending down completed models via the mail or on train trips. During this period they rented a studio which they shared with one of Trish's jeweller friends and Bob Naismith, another silversmith who also did early miniature design work for Citadel miniatures.

In 1986 Morrison was offered a full-time position at Citadel miniatures and, hoping to buy a house with Trish, accepted the job. The pair moved south and joined the Citadel design studio at Enfield Chambers in Nottingham.

In 1988, as part of an initiative by Bryan Ansell to diversify the miniatures that Games Workshop sold, and to diffuse criticism of the growing commercial juggernaut that Games Workshop was becoming, Aly and Trish founded Marauder Miniatures. In practise this was a wholly-owned subsidiary of Games Workshop, since it relied on Citadel's manufacturing and distribution facilities, but Aly and Trish had the freedom to develop the studio as they saw fit and earned a sales commission.

To say that Marauder was an enduring line would be an understatement. The Marauder dwarf troll slayers were never replaced, and are still the current miniature for Warhammer: the Old World - arguably they're the design archetype underlying the Age of Sigmar Fyreslayer range. While Trish carved out a niche as the mother of monsters, Aly's designs capture whimsy and wit, models with the exaggerated animation of a Jim Henson puppet..

Trish and Aly had one child together, Mharaid, whose birth in 1992 was announced in issue 150 of White Dwarf on the new page, under the whimsical heading "New Marauder Miniature".

Morrison was an active part of model design at Games Workshop until his retirement in May 2026. His blog, Aly's Toy Soldiers, describes ongoing difficulties with the chronic condition fibromyalgia, though we do not know if this played any role in his death.

Writing to her own Facebook group, Trish Carden says  "Mharaid and I are heartbroken to announce the passing of Aly Morrison, a very much loved father, veteran wargames miniatures designer and friend to many around the tabletop and the world. Aly passed unexpectedly but peacefully this Wednesday, and will be sorely missed". She requests that people respect their privacy during this time of mourning, but "would love and appreciate to hear any stories those that knew him have to tell of their times together".

In writing this obituary I've relied extensively on Trish Carden's interview with John Stallard and Robin Dews in the collection 'Talking Miniatures', and her posts in her Facebook group. The Lost Minis Wiki was also a big help.

title: [Warmachine] Competitive Innovations in the Iron Kingdoms: WTC, Lock & Load, and the End of 2026 Meta
content:
The end of the Warmachine event year is defined by two events:

  • Warmachine WTC (World Teams Championship)
  • Lock & Load US (Premier Steamforged Games run end of year Iron Gauntlet)

While drastically different approaches are required for both formats, they equally encourage the best of the best to hone what has emerged as the top of the meta. The sea of releases this year has certainly been a challenge for top tournament players to navigate but some clear winners did emerge.

Credit: Steamforged Games

World Team Championship 2026

First was WTC, the global showcase of skill and prowess from countries across continents with several countries bringing multiple teams. Going into the event the obvious meta front runners were Grymkin, Old Umbrey, and the new meta powerhouse Fane of Nyrro. As such it was assumed they would dominate the overall meta representation, which was remarkably not the case.

Outside of Thornfall Alliance and other Armies of Legend whose results are statistically insignificant, the most popular armies at WTC, Old Umbrey and Wicked Harvest, demonstrated why they were taken so often as they put up solid win rates despite being known quantities that define the metagame, although their win rates were not out of bounds. The other big winners were Brineblood Marauders, Orgoth Sea Raiders and Dark Operations, all of which certainly outperformed the win rates of several more popular armies. These armies were probably very well positioned to fight into the established metagame and carve success out of a crowded field where the more popular armies could be easily predicted. These are also older armies often piloted by dedicated players, so there can easily be something of an experience difference compared to the newer, more popular armies, particularly in cases where the pilots of the newer armies were not as well-practiced into the likes of Dark Operations or Sea Raiders, allowing them to submarine into impressive performances despite their small caster stables.

The biggest losers, win rate-wise, were House Kallyss, Gravediggers and Winter Korps. Gravediggers and Winter Korps have a very gun-focused army plan in a meta dominated by Morosov and Old Witch and thus very hostile into shooting. They also currently demonstrate limited caster variety based on how much Baranov and Cyn were in the field, which made them easier to plan for than armies with a wider stable of viable casters. The popularity of House Kallyss was probably the biggest surprise of the WTC statistics, but those were mostly dominated by Tyrus/Hellyth pairings. Although the pairing was strong and can be successful (as discussed later), it ended up being another known quantity that had questionable success into the major bogeymen armies of the event.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Fane of Nyrro was probably the biggest surprise in terms of expectations vs reality of their popularity and success rate, as many predicted that they would be the most popular and dominating faction of the event, but there are a couple of asterisks to this point. The first being that Fane did not have all of their in-app tools available. Harasheth was a legal model due to his Warmachine 3D version, but the rest of his box was not, and getting access to powerful models like the Riven and Styrge Hounds would have certainly changed the game. The other asterisk is that Nymara, as a caster, had an absurdly strong 67% win rate, with the dismal performance of the other Fane casters bringing the overall stats into the realm of reasonable. Nymara was a popular and powerful choice throughout both of the year’s capstone events and is absolutely a caster to watch.

The winning team, Australia Charging Cassowaries, had an eclectic mix of armies, being one of the rare teams to double up on their factions with two House Kallyss players as well as Grymkin, Old Umbrey and Winter Korps. The off-meta choices continue into the individual list choices as the Grymkin pairing does not contain Old Witch and although Morosov and Lissya were common sights at the event, both those lists have unique spins with Lissya’s extra-heavy cohort build and Morosov’s shifters heavily favoring werewolves over the more common werebears.

The pairing process and performance of the winners indicates that the Cassowaries were well aware of the meta and made their choices deliberately to counter the expected meta. Perhaps the most pronounced examples of this are the double Dusk lists. Hazaroth seems to have explicitly been the Fane of Nyrro drop as Hazaroth was played into it 3 times and going 2-1, while Dan Tacken’s Hellyth list came loaded for bear with an impressive 4 drops into Old Umbrey, going 3-1 in that matchup. The wolf-heavy Morosov list appears to have been built for Grymkin, dropping into Old Witch twice. Finally, Robin de Oliveira’s Heretic/King of Nothing pairing must have presented significant pairing challenges for all of the Grymkin drops that were mostly prepared for Old Witch, going 5-0 and taking the coveted number 2 spot on the individual players list. Although the list has no bearing on the results and shouldn’t be used as a pure indication of player skill given the WTC matchup process, it’s still very impressive for a list with 240 names on it.

Lock and Load US

Lock & Load US is characterized by the now legendary Iron Gauntlet which people have been qualifying for throughout the year at their local aptly named Iron Gauntlet Qualifiers. The format is an iron man event, which is to say players are separated into pods and those pods feed their top players into a final single elimination event where winner takes all.

Out of the 32 qualified players who decided to attend we see a fairly warped trend of stats. Players of this skill level made a true mix of understandable and baffling army choices. Was it just their own personal comfort pick? A back pocket favorite to have fun with? The deliberate attempt to attack this brutal gauntlet with a dark horse choice? Let's dig in and find out!

Dread Armada were obviously the breakout stars, with four players (including the ultimate winner) getting an army printed out in the scant week between the files going live and Lock and Load happening. Wicked Harvest, Gravediggers and especially Fane of Nyrro, now in possession of all of their tools except those announced at the event itself, made up fully half of the top 32, with the others split fairly evenly between most of the other factions and a few Armies of Legend to keep things interesting. Notable at this level is the complete absence of Sea Raiders or Shadowflame Shard as representatives of the wholly new armies released since the start of Mk4. Although none of the Gravediggers players advanced, which was predictable based on their poor performance at the WTC, the Wicked Harvest going 0 for 4 into the top 16 was a bit surprising, but there is a reason for this.

Credit: Steamforged Games

Interestingly, the meta that so defined the WTC team formation and results appears largely absent in the top 16 of the Iron Gauntlet. By contrast, several of the armies on display are either very new (Dread Armada, Fane including new post-WTC models such as the Styrge Hounds and Styrge Abhorreth) or are older armies of legend that are bringing their classic tools to bear in the current game (Devourer’s Host, Ravens of War). It appears that, taking some lessons from WTC about the risks of playing into a predictable meta, several of the players instead opted to try and ambush opponents with options that opponents may not have had the opportunity or time to practice against, leading to a lot of improvisational decision making. When expecting a single elimination format, forcing your opponent to think even more about what you have brought is a valuable edge.

While the broader meta is split between newer and much older armies, the top end of the of the meta seems to be defined by front-line personal work casters, with Terminus, Nymara and Dekathus all dominating the top end and Vorsalys being a choice to try to keep those melee monsters in check. By contrast, more back-line casters like Shadowtongue, Vorgoroth, Vayl and Harasheth did not find corresponding success, all being defeated by the front-line powerhouses. It appears that Wicked Harvest was also fairly vulnerable to these powerful front-liners, whose aggressive play and innate resilience appeared to push the little nightmares out of the top cut. Combined with Old Witch being slated for a power reduction and the most successful Grymkin list at WTC being Witch-less, it will be interesting to see how Grymkin builds will adjust into 2027.

The final match was a battle of the new stuff, with the all new Dread Armada army led by Terminus and piloted by Dan Riker finding success against Peyton Preece’s Vorsalys, who was packing his own brand new toys in two Styrge Abhorreths (soon eager to try the even newer models revealed at the event itself to be sure). The combination of Entropic Shroud and Aegis in the Terminus list reducing most enemy spell ranges to effectively zero appears to be a big part of allowing Terminus to retain his threatening agency against a field where powerful control effects were common.

Image Credit: Steamforged Games

Warmachine in 2026 was one of the most tumultuous competitively. Between the official release of four full armies, the re-release of three more, and a rare mid-year update the overall meta felt like it was changing weekly. The armies and archetypes of gunlines and aggressive anti-gunlines were systematically replaced with aggressive mid board bullies that could play wide in sub-packages and silos. Spheres of control and combat around very widely spread out objectives. While exciting to learn about as new rules were revealed the added complications of new mechanics was exciting to many and suffocating to others. While Lock and load had some distinct surprises and the podium of WTC deviated from American expectations, many hope the 2027 meta is more stable. More armies that feel in line with the new SFG style of mechanics not simply propped up by highly skilled faction experts. Warmachine has been coming back with a vengeance, and as far as army updates/additions were concerned, 2026 was an explosion of accessibility, so we hope things even out with the new update so everyone can play this awesome game their way.

title: Magic: The Gathering release schedule 2026-2027
content:
What is the current MTG release schedule? This guide tracks all of the upcoming MTG releases in 2026-2027, including release dates, mechanics, and story details. This year, we saw crossovers with Star Trek and the Hobbit , plus a 'What If?' set shaking up the multiverse.

Then in 2027, we're going to a new ocean plane, seeing a massive battle between mechs and monsters on Kamigawa, and finally we get more than a glimpse at what's been going on in Zhalfir recently.

While you're filling in your calendar, our complete history of all MTG sets in order of release might come in useful too. Below we've collected all the available Magic: The Gathering release dates and windows for 2026 and 2027 - starting with the upcoming releases, then moving on to the most recent.

Here's the Magic: The Gathering 2026/2027 release schedule:

  • Lorwyn Eclipsed - January 23, 2026
  • Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - March 6, 2026
  • Secrets of Strixhaven - April 24, 2026
  • Marvel Superheroes - June 26, 2026
  • The Hobbit - August 14, 2026
  • Reality Fracture - October 2, 2026
  • Star Trek - November 11, 2026
  • Mystery Booster Commander Edition - November 13, 2026
  • Nauctis: The Sunken Realm - February 5, 2027
  • Marvel: Darkhold Destiny - April 9, 2027
  • Kamigawa: Titanbreach - June 4, 2027
  • Zhalfir - October 1, 2027

Upcoming set release dates

Star Trek - November 13, 2026

There are seven Standard-legal sets this year, good grief! There have been rumors of a Star Trek set swirling around for years, and it looks like WotC has finally decided to… make it so.

2026 marks Star Trek's 60th anniversary, and this release will explore the entire history of the show, in its every iteration. Obviously,  Spacecraft cards are back and new mechanics encouraging diverse creature types and making choices highlight this franchise's core themes.

Magic has already proven it can jump genres and tackle sci-fi settings, and Star Trek certainly has enough content to produce a working set. That said, the whole ethos of Star Trek seems kind of antithetical to a combat-based TCG. Not to mention: those planeswalkers are violating the Prime Directive all the time.

1/4

Nauctis: The Sunken Realm - February 5, 2027

The first new set of 2027 takes us under the sea and to a brand new plane. Nauctis: The Sunken Realm explores a water world and takes place entirely beneath the wave. While sea creatures are usually Blue's domain, this fishy focus allows Wizards to flesh out a full color pie of marine life.

You can expert merfolk galore, but also some more unusual fantasy races like puffer fish people, penguin people, crab men, walrus women, and something that I would swear was an underwater sliver, if it didn't have the wrong number of limbs.

WotC is leaning hard into high fantasy with Nauctis, which should be exciting for anyone tiring of all the genre exploration of recent years. Kelp takes the place of forests, there's a new sea-based evasion mechanic that's equivalent to flying, and all the humans are stuck in diving suits and submarines.

All these sea creatures make it a great set for biology nerds like me too. There are undead monsters based on whalefall - I'm in love!

1/4

Marvel: Darkhold Destiny - April 9, 2027

The third Marvel Magic set features all the mystical, magical, and supernatural characters that haven't yet been given much time in the spotlight, from Blade to Doctor Strange.

In a truly interesting twist, this will be the first Universes Beyond to feature an original narrative, which Wizards cooked up in conjunction with Marvel. It even includes a brand new comic book character.

We've already had a few cards teased, which reveal Arcane spells are back, there's a new card type 'Dimensions', and we're getting books-matters mechanics for the first time ever.

1/3

Kamigawa Titanbreach - June 4, 2027

Worlds are at war. Ikoria has collided with Kamigawa, and it's time for an inter-planar showdown. As soon as Wizards started linking planes with Omenpaths, we knew it was only a matter of time before we got a 'Pacific Rim' set, and the hype for Kamigawa: Titanbreach is immediately off the chain. Big mechs, big monsters, two beloved Magic settings shown off to their fullest. What's not to like?

I only have two questions. Is this where we'll finally see Battles make their return? And why did they lead with Aetherdrift instead of this?

Zhalfir - October 1, 2027

Zhalfir is a setting we've been eagerly waiting to see, ever since it phased back into existence at the end of March of the Machine. Now it's getting its own set, providing a fresh take on an old Magic: The Gathering setting.

Longtime players will no doubt find some things familiar about Zhalfir - for instance, a new Teferi legendary creature card is all but guaranteed. However, this is a deeper look at Zhalfir than we ever got when it was part of Dominaria, promising Magic's take on African culture and mythology.

Zhalfir has replaced Mirrodin/New Phyrexia, and it's lit by Mirrodin's five suns, which makes it a land of endless day. Contrasting that is a spirit realm, a dark land full of danger but also a connection to your ancestors. Overall Zhalfir promises to be a visually stunning new world with amazing architecture and fashion - and great hair!

Latest releases in 2026

Lorwyn Eclipsed - January 23, 2026

Lorwyn Eclipsed was the first set of 2026, a long-awaited return to this Celtic folklore inspired world that's every bit as beloved as Kamigawa or Tarkir. That title is a reference to the new identity of the plane. While the twin realities of Lorwyn and Shadowmoor used to alternate every 300 years, they've now fused together.

While Lorwyn is a land of eternal day and flower-filled meadows, Shadowmoor is one of endless night. This set showed off the setting in its new, combined state: part-spooky, part-nice, with its denizens shifting between two forms as the borders of the two worlds constantly move. To show that duality, Lorwyn Eclipsed is full of double-faced cards that you can pay mana to transform.

This release maintained a lot of what fans love about this MTG plane, namely the non-human races of the kithkin, faeries, elves, and merfolk. There are even a few Kindred spells!

Interestingly, this set also introduced us to the new first-year characters from Strixhaven. Are they this phase's protagonists?

Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles - March 6, 2026

Revealed slightly later than the rest of the 2026 calendar, the second release of the year was MTG Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. Featuring all your favorite heroes and villains, from Krang to April O'Neil, there's some fun stuff in here - including art from the original comic books and lands based on pizza toppings. It did put me off cheese for at least a week, though.

This was a smaller set, like the Spider-Man release that got such a frosty reception last year. However, the TMNT set came with more interesting side products, including a single five-color Commander precon (here's a handy upgrade guide for you) and a new 'Turtle Team Up' box that provides a cooperative way to play Magic.

Secrets of Strixhaven - April 24, 2026

Secrets of Strixhaven was our second look at this magical school, and featured the five distinct colleges once again - each of which had its own precon. This set introduces some new characters enrolling in the academy, and follows up on the fan-favorites who've just graduated.

While Secrets didn't try to reinvent the mold, it did see us step outside the walls of Strixhaven for the first time. Instead of moving back home to save on rent or cramming like sardines into a shared apartment, the new graduates were using their arcane skills to explore the wider world of Arcavios and broker magical peace treaties.

Secrets of Strixhaven also launched alongside a novel by Seanan Mcguire - the first Magic book in a long while!

Marvel Superheroes - June 26, 2026

Marvel Superheroes launched right as Summer kicked into gear. Perhaps the largest of several planned Magic: The Gathering Marvel sets, it seems Wizards of the Coast has packed in as many characters as they can, from the Avengers, to The Fantastic Four, to Daredevil. And of course, Squirrel Girl is making an appearance for the squirrel tribal lovers.

There's also a Jumpstart release for this set: themed packs that players can mash together into an instant deck. As both UB and Jumpstart are aimed at new players, WotC is experimenting with combining the two concepts.

Marvel Super Heroes is out in the wild now, with dozens of legendary creatures doing super-powered battle, from Marvel greats like Iron Man to obscure heroes like Reptil. In fact, there are so many characters here that honestly we have to wonder what's been left on the table for future releases. We were guessing X-Men would be coming in 2027, but this set features Wolverine, Storm, and Quicksilver.

Another new development for this set is that it's playable on Arena! Seems Wizards renegotiated its deal with Marvel, allowing now the Marvel cards to join Magic's digital platform in a Snap. Ahem.

The Hobbit - August 14, 2026

There wasn't enough content in The Hobbit for a satisfying film trilogy, but there seems to be enough to make a strong card set, even if it needed some padding out with random animals. This second Middle Earth set features plenty of new versions of characters we've seen before - such as Gandalf, Bilbo, Gollum, and Elrond - with important reprints like Tom Bombadil and The One Ring appearing as box-toppers.

The Hobbit had lots of new stuff to be excited about too. Dwarves made a big appearance - a fantasy race that's often been unkindly ignored by Magic lore in the past. Smaug is also here with several different commanders that are all terrifying treasure-makers, and the stone trolls have a surprisingly powerful card too.

Reality Fracture - October 2, 2026

Reality Fracture was a What If? set, where we got to meet alternate versions of existing characters. Jace went full supervillain and made new versions of his pals: a fiery Ajani, ice Chandra, Benalian healer Liliana, and chain-veil wielding Garruk.

In fact, he built an entire 'Echoverse'. It's not just the planeswalkers. There are opposite versions of characters and creatures too. Instead of Tinybones there's Titanbones. Instead of Craterhoof, there's a red Craterclaw that cares about artifacts.

The set takes place on Hexhaven, a more combat-focused version of Strixhaven, where Jace has control and seemingly rules with an iron fist, with his own faceless enforcers and eyeball-creature sentinels.

Wizards cleverly made sure to include regular and Echoverse versions of the same characters in each pack, so that you didn't have to be a Magic lore expert to .

Mystery Booster: Commander Edition - October 19, 2026

A surprise latecomer to the 2026 release schedule, Mystery Booster: Commander Edition seems designed to delight EDH fans with unlikely throwbacks like a new Joven card, as well as weird and wacky rulebreaker commanders. There are eight of these in total, and each one lets players bend the commander deckbuilding rules in unique ways - such as adding instants and sorcery cards of an additional color.

Like past Mystery Boosters, this set is designed to be drafted. And like past Mystery Boosters, it'll be available at MagicCons or as Festivals in a Box.

If you're into more than just trading card games, then we can tell you what other products Wizards of the Coast is releasing this year. Head to our DnD release schedule guide for the latest on the world's biggest tabletop RPG.

title: Pathfinder publisher disputes claims of AI art in its latest book, Feybound
content:
Feybound, a Pathfinder sourcebook released on November 4, has come under fire for allegedly containing AI artwork. The offending images were first flagged by fans on Reddit on November 10. However, Paizo has told Wargamer "we have discussed the concerns raised with the artist responsible for the art in Feybound, and the artist denies using AI".

The Reddit post highlights seven illustrations as supposed evidence. The listed 'signs' of generative AI include temple pillars that lack symmetry, impossible architecture, and animals and people melting together in strange, unsightly ways.

However, Paizo tells Wargamer that, following its investigation, "the art director supports the artist, who has produced a lot of material for Paizo over the years." "Paizo does not use AI art in our products, and all artists sign a contract with a clear exclusion of using artificial intelligence in their creations", it adds.

Paizo's policy on generative AI is well-known and long-standing. Back in 2023, a blog post titled Paizo and Artificial Intelligence stated: "Paizo will not use AI-generated 'creative' work of any kind for the foreseeable future". "The ethical and legal issues surrounding "AI art" and writing prompt programs-and the serious threat they pose to the livelihoods of partners who have helped us get to where we are today as a company-demand that we take a firm position against the use of this technology in Paizo products."

That same post asserts that Paizo's creative contracts require all submitted work to be human-made. "Our customers expect a human touch to our releases, and so long as the ethical and legal circumstances surrounding these programs remains murky and undefined, we are unwilling to associate our brands with the technology in any way", it adds.

"Stated plainly-when you buy a Paizo product, you can be sure that it is the work of human professionals who have spent years honing their craft to produce the best work we can."

Whatever your opinion of the artwork in question, the scenario shines light on a sad truth for artists and publishers. As generative AI continues to train on the stolen work of artists, its presence gets harder to police. AI art isn't simply stealing creative ideas and economic opportunities from real artists. It's also subjecting them to intense, sometimes unfair scrutiny, as the general public attempts to root out the AI wrongdoers that policy might have missed.

Still, Paizo says to its community: "thanks for bringing it to our attention", and reminds us it "takes alleged use of AI products in our art seriously".

If you'd like to talk more about the best tabletop RPGs in the business, join us for a chat in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Magic: The Gathering Star Trek Review, Part 2 of 4 – Multicolor & Colorless Cards
content:
Space, the final frontier. These are the voyages of the starship Enterprise...as well as around 34 other new Spaceraft. Our continuing mission: To explore in detail the ramifications of newly-printed cardboard; to speculate upon their effects on formats such as Commander, Standard, & Modern; to boldly joke about the 43 new Creature types printed in this set unlikely ever to be seen again! Yes, Star Trek has arrived to Magic, and with it a host of new cards sure to shake things up. Most impactful is the full realization of Spacecraft as an Artifact subtype, more than doubling the number thusly printed. Today we're covering the set's multicolor and colorless cards.

Star Trek officially releases to tabletop on November 13th, and on Magic: The Gathering Arena on November 10th.

Multicolor

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Borg Cube

Saffgor: This card is indeed strong, but has one clear caveat—its ability does not carry over if the Cube re-enters, is copied, etc. This is also a linked ability, meaning that if you give this Escape or Delve somehow, those cards cannot be Assimilated. What this card doesn't say keeps it from being truly potent, but its actual text is quite good. Just don't overthink this one, it has guardrails.

BPhillipYork:  This is honestly really disappointing, the Borg Cube took on the whole Federation fleet, this would lose to the Defiant, which it... did not. It really feels like it should get +1/+1 for each charge counter it has one it or something. The exile and then assimilate is nice, but for 7 mana it's not that impressive. Granted it's basically another Meteor Golem type effect, but it requires 2 colored mana.

FromTheShire: Especially with the colored mana cost you're not likely to be casting this for free but a decent reduction is reasonable. The ability is also solid, though it's not exactly quick.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The City on the Edge of Forever

Saffgor: I kind of wish this could sit in the Command Zone, or otherwise be more findable, because the ability to stop things from phasing in is rather unique. There's a ton of removal which becomes all the more permanent with that effect onboard, and the card itself is at worse some card draw and a temporary board clear.

BPhillipYork: This is kind of crazy, like if you can protect that admittedly 0/1 creature, it just locks your opponents boards out. And it's 5 mana, which is more than a basic wrath, but only 1 more. Potentially really strong asymmetric board wipe if you have a plan for it.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dal R'El, Augment Orphan

Saffgor: Gruul Lotus Cobra in the Command Zone with a mana outlet to draw the deck alongside a Drownyard Temple? Shoot, yeah this seems incredibly potent. It's likely only going to get better once we see the eventual X-Men set with Mutant support, so keep Dal in mind.

BPhillipYork: Well, good another Lotus Cobra. Landfall wasn't strong enough already. This is really great for, like, good decks. With fetch lands alone it's a massive boost early to build some momentum and if you are fetching more lands or ramping aggressively it gets really gross.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dathon, His Heart Open

Saffgor: Appearing in the sole episode of Star Trek I've actually seen, this guy is a very cool take on Temur. Sagas isn't something the identity has had a Commander for thus far (explicitly, anyway) and that activated ability being for any Enchantment means things like Gardenize or Simic Ascendancy are very real here. Saffgor, His Interest Piqued.

FromTheShire: Temur enchantments seems like a neat deck to build. I'm not sure I'd actually go the Saga route since I still tend to dislike them in Commander, and I'm not sure you'll cast enough of them for the 2 damage per to do more than annoy your opponents and draw aggro, but maybe that's actually a viable choice once you put it all together.

BPhillipYork: I'm really glad they referenced this, one of the better Star Trek episodes. A Temur enchantress that also deals damage when you play Sagas is fun, and great to build around. The ability to place counters is also really useful in random ways. Fun card.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Hit It!

Saffgor: Aside from the weird Day 0 errata which doesn't change this card's functional text, it's cool to have such a versatile ramp piece. Haste is great, mill is great, and the fact this will usually be able to find a nonbasic means it can help colorfix in RGx lists. I expect to see this wherever Haste is relevant, in the appropriate colors.

FromTheShire: Now we're talking. Rhythm of the Wild has seen play in a bunch of formats, and it's not for making your creatures uncounterable. Haste is excellent, and having ramp stapled on to get to your big threats faster is a great bonus.

BPhillipYork: This is fine but Gruul really has better all haste sources to use.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Inner Light

Saffgor: It's a bit slow, but my goodness that's a lot of value. At minimum a reanimation, probably some card draw, and possibly some lifegain and a Treasure. If you expect to see every chapter, and do something with it, this card is backbreaking.

BPhillipYork: I really sort of hate that second Saga effect whenever I see it. Potentially you can like, slap double strike on something or else generate extra combat steps, but it's usually just draw 1 card potentially, which isn't very significant. Yet it seems to show up a lot on Sagas and such, I don't know why. Anyway, another great episode, okay card.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Kira Nerys, Firebrand

Saffgor: Star Trek's greatest achievement by my mark is the introduction of compelling Spacecraft in the Command Zone, and multiple cool Boros options. Kira is the standout for that latter camp, and is utterly bonkers when built around. Sneak Attack, blink, tokens, you name it; she's got a number of viable build paths at all power levels, and I expect to sit across from her at the LGS and MagicCons.

FromTheShire: Well that is just terrifying to sit down across from. Even worse than hasty threats are ones that enter attacking. It doesn't have to be attacking the same player as the attacking creature either, so this is a great way to cheat things in around defensive enchantments and the like.

BPhillipYork: The ability to have creatures enter after blockers are declared is pretty nasty, but it's also pretty transparent, so it's going to lead to people not wanting to be attacked by you, and lead to your creatures just being blown up. Definitely you can like, Sneak Attack out a Blightsteel Colossus and kill someone, but once you do that nobody is going to suffer you to attack them.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Mirror Universe Intrusion

Saffgor: If you rate Imposter Mech reasonably, this is along those lines. You'll rarely kick this, but having the option is nice I suppose. Really though, this exists to snag opposing value bodies and tutors.

BPhillipYork: I love this. I love the whole trope of, oh the evil version just has facial hair. And of course, the mirror universe version is the same but menacing. Chef's kiss. It's pretty good for just cloning your opponents commander or other super useful creature, and the kicker is only good if they have a creature based deck.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Nog, Ambitious Cadet

Saffgor: Build-your-own Icetill Explorer, sure. The real issue stems from the fact that, should Nog ever be removed, you are so wildly far behind. Paying in installments feels great until you need to do it twice. That said, using this with Agatha's Soul Cauldron and Creatures that are already Scouts? That has potential!

BPhillipYork: 6 mana for additional land and play lands from the yard, effectively. It's fine, but it also curves kind of badly. If you drop him turn 2, unless you managed a dork on turn 1, then turn 3 you are forced to pay the 1 and probably can't pay the 3, so you're on a 2-turn delay to get what you came for.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Sarek, Federation Ambassador

Saffgor: This just seems like a pain to track with not that much payoff. Ooh, a fair win condition if I do the thing, spooky. No thanks.

BPhillipYork: There are some goofy creatures that have a bunch of creature types, like Curious Farm Animals or Stonework Packbeast that come to mind, so if you want to make like a weird bad deck that is sort of fun. Run stuff from the D&D set and play a lot of cards that don't usually see play, he's good for that. Otherwise, probably pass.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Seven of Nine

Saffgor: Seven is the defacto Dilemma Commander unless you want to play 5c, and she's a decent one (if not a bit boring). I talked about Dilemmas at length in a recent Puzzlebox, so my full thoughts are there, but the real shock is how fair Seven actually ends up being, unless you do something silly with Pyramids.

BPhillipYork: Well this is potentially pretty strong, though it's really just an enabler for the true dilemma commander Captain Benjamin Sisko.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Warp Speed

Saffgor: They had to make this Simic identity I guess, what a shame. This is an absolutely tremendous spin on Spelunking, and the ability to translate it into advantage later is very welcome.

FromTheShire: Pretty much any card that makes your lands enter untapped has seen play somewhere because it's a wildly powerful ability. You may remember there was even a whole Modern deck about it. I'm not sure if there is enough that dovetails with this in Standard outside of Evendo, Waking Haven to be a real thing just yet, but I could see it possibly swapping in for The Wandering Minstrel in Pioneer Scapeshift since it doesn't die to Fatal Push.

BPhillipYork: Personally I don't think making lands enter untapped is all that exciting, most of the lands that enter tapped are bad. Cards that make bad cards less bad is not really my thing, but there are things you can do, especially with the bounce lands, and that's where I could see this being good.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain Benjamin Sisko

Saffgor: There's a few ways to face infinite Dilemmas, but honestly this reads more like the mandated 'play all the cards in the set' 5c Commander. I guess we need to have it so fans of the property can slop it up, but I dunno, this one really doesn't spark joy.

BPhillipYork: Well this is obviously the build a dilemma deck commander, and I think a deck with tons of charms and stuff is a fun way to play. It's not super good, but it'll let you interact with the board a lot in different ways.

Colorless

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Combadge

Saffgor: Combadge isn't impressive, but the fact it makes a token Equipment matters immensely for a new Commander from the set, Gwyndala, the Progeny. That's where you'll see it, and it's pretty fantastic with her.

BPhillipYork: So, uh, 7 mana to make something unblockable. Well, it's really 7 mana to make 2 things unblockable, but even so.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Deep Space 9

Saffgor: It never becomes a Creature so alas, it cannot be your Commander. Regardless, this does some asinine things when cloned, in much the same vein as Gyruda. If this resolves, things get nasty, but ultimately it is just a big stupid Artifact.

FromTheShire: It's slow but it's pretty funny in a Primal Surge style deck. It's so expensive you definitely better be cheating it out somehow.

BPhillipYork: It's not like, super good, but it's a fun kind of, generate a ton of colorless mana, and then who knows what will show up. Probably Eldrazi.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Replicator

Saffgor: Things that make token copies will be playing this, as generally the upfront cost and/or opportunity cost of cloning something is more than the repeated cost of Replicator. Great thing to use with the New Planet tokens in the set as well.

FromTheShire: That's a lot of words to say Populate unless you're doing something unique to make token copies of noncreatures.

BPhillipYork: Making Food tokens isn't very exciting, but there are lots of ways to copy permanent spells now and this would let you make even more copies, which could get really nasty. So it's a great further enabler for a deck based on making token versions of things that don't normally have them.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class

Saffgor: This is a reasonable Spacecraft and will see you at minimum one additional card per turn, but where this might be enjoyed as a Commander is in some sort of Proliferate+Flash enabler deck. If you can add counters on opponents' turns, and Flash the cards you exile out, it becomes a cool value engine.

BPhillipYork: This seems fine, there's way you can get around the sorcery limitation, such as proliferate, and that'll let you play more stuff off the top, and certainly tap a creature to get the ability to play the top card of your deck is solid enough.

Land

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Starfleet Academy

Saffgor: You need to control 7+ types for this to start going mana-positive, and that's both fairly easy, and fairly difficult. I think in any Creature-heavy deck that isn't typal, you can probably turn this on in a meaningful capacity, but you're probably already way ahead on board at that point.

FromTheShire: The vast majority of the time this is probably not going to pay off, and will instead warp your deck trying to jump through hoops.

BPhillipYork: That's a very solid land, enters untapped and potentially makes a lot of mana, and unlike Gaea's Cradle variants it's not only green.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Anomalyland Cycle

Saffgor: These seem...pretty damn good. They remain mana-neutral, colorfix and get you a Landfall trigger, and many of their effects are pretty much at-rate for Land abilities. Green one is the stand-out, but Artificial Anomaly isn't too far off of Ramunap Ruins, and that card was banned in Standard.

FromTheShire: The crucial difference is that Ruins sacrificed a different land than itself, and was red. That made it perfect for pushing through the last few points of damage with aggro red after the board stabilized, and with Artificial Anomaly being in black I don't think it's as useful. Black has good ways to remove creatures so that board stall doesn't happen, and right now the most successful Rakdos deck is Lizards, which I can assure you in my games has either won or lost by the time you are at this plus 4 other lands. As a cycle they're not bad, I think we're more likely to see one or two ofs in a few decks rather than being major players.

BPhillipYork: These are fine, not terribly exciting, though I guess if you have the ability to play from your yard and the game stalls out you can just keep using them over and over, and end up with a lot of new planet tokens. I could see using Artificial Anomaly as a way of dealing consistent damage by having the ability to play lands from your graveyard in the right deck.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dilemmaland Cycle

Saffgor: These being slowlands means they likely go more in Commander than 60-card, but Quark's Bar being an extra, potentially-untapped ping on a Red Land is frightening. Great to see a Rare Land cycle that works in Monocolor, but these not being fetchable like their Surveilland counterparts is a shame.

BPhillipYork: Quark's Bar is potentially usable in Worldgorger Dragon / Animate Dead loops as a damage source, and it's a slight improvement on the other ones that are deserts, other than that though these are all kind of meh to me for general usage.

Commander

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Borg Queen

Saffgor: This seems...mediocre. Theft in general is always a tough thing because you lose resources as players are eliminated, and The Borg Queen clearly wants you to be a board-based midrange deck. She can't even mill your opponents out, as the rest get put back rather than remaining in exile. Just not a great card, unfortunately, especially at a whopping 7 mana.

BPhillipYork: Well, there she is. Commander for your Borg deck, and she does something on ETB which is nice, since I think with a built in anthem and that ability to assimilate every attack she's going to be blown up a lot.  At 7 mana you're probably not casting her a lot of times per game.

FromTheShire: For 7 mana you don't even get to hit each opponent? Not great, Jim.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Commander Spock

Saffgor: 'Random bullshit go' is a strange theme for the logic-themed character Spock is, but with all the tutor-to-top effects in Bant, it might be less random than you think. Spock can crack tutor piles quite well in fact, especially if we're making our own little pile with Congregation at Dawn. He scales in power based on targets to hit, which means he's viable across a number of brackets, too—the more I think on this card, the more I like it.

BPhillipYork: This is really solid. Kind of weird, but basically at a minimum it's draw a card, and then gets better from there. Bant ramps really well and can fill out lots of differently named lands fast, to make this a lot more powerful. And you can just flicker him a bunch.

FromTheShire: Solid effect, but only getting one trigger per turn unless you're flickering and needing to survive combat as a 3/5 isn't outstanding. The fact it keys off of the lands you have in play means you're not doing the normal plan of trying to cheat out something giant with your free cast either so it's basically a value play unless you're stacking combo pieces on the top.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Jean-Luc Picard, Luminary

Saffgor: It goes without saying, but rest in peace to the wonderful Patrick Stewart. It is a shame his face Commander card is mediocre. We'll talk about it in a bit, but placing counters on Spacecraft is worse than simply building your deck with enough high-power Creatures to turbo-Station them, and that draw trigger is shockingly restrained. He's fine, but we can do better.

BPhillipYork: Drawing off 3 cost mana rocks is pretty great, and leads to an overabundance of resources scenario that get's really dangerous. A Jeskai artifact commander like this is basically just an improvement over Jhoira, Weatherlight Captain or at least a strong variant, and it's not that hard to get some artifact cost reduction and just draw out your deck.

FromTheShire: Yeah I think this deck ends up being built not to care about Spacecraft unfortunately, it's just a pile of artifact cost reducers and huge payoffs since you have 'everything is a cantrip' in the Command Zone and storm/combo decks love that.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Worf, Defiant Commander

Saffgor: I think Worf just ends up being too fair, as even with extra combats he's less mana-efficient for a similar role to the Mardu Zuko. Not compelling.

BPhillipYork: This is pretty solid. With things like melee and myriad you can be attacking everyone all the time and just keep rolling out more and more aggression, which is very Worf-y. Actually it's not, Worf's main job on Star Trek was to get thrown around to prove how strong some alien was. But it's who Worf wanted to be.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Alexander, Ship's Fool

Saffgor: Oh this guy is just wonderful. A Boros Vial-Smasher of sorts, with some group hug/slug elements, and mana-value matters. We're going to be untapping this guy, placing big stuff on top, just having a blast. They were incredibly generous to make this an Instant-speed tap ability!

BPhillipYork: That's fun.

FromTheShire: Now this I like. Random damage and political tool for the ultimate "hey guys it's not my fault you took damage and look at that scary Blightsteel Steve just drew" table manipulation. If you're a bard at heart, I think you're going to have a blast with this guy.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain Janeway, Endgame

Saffgor: Officer typal is probably just better done by the 5c Sisko, and that unblockable ability is laughably inefficient. No thanks.

BPhillipYork: This is fun, not great but lots of ways to make Officers and throwing them away for more card draw is very thematic.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Captain Kirk, Boldly Going

Saffgor: Tutoring up a pretty good Spacecraft which he in turn helps to turbo out and pump, which in turn causes it to draw more cards? I mean, shoot, this guy does everything. Just make sure that the Enterprise doesn't get exiled, and Kirk here takes care of the rest. The Spock precon knows how to design a Commander, and probably has two of the best options on its own!

BPhillipYork: Crazy ramp commander really. That particular Enterprise is really good, and uh, goes really well with crazy ramp. Kind of weird to have a pure value commander, though you could definitely make a Spacecraft tribal deck which would be kind of fun.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Chief Kyle, Transporter Tech

Saffgor: Seeing 'Kyle' on a Magic card makes my hackles raise, but for what it's worth he's quite strong. Combining Landfall & blink with so many Creatures like sad robot which find Lands is sure to lead to an outpouring of value.

BPhillipYork: This is an okay variant for Brago, King Eternal, a little slower but maybe less dangerous, and of course you can just run both. It can be a value play early that turns into a win con later which is pretty solid.

FromTheShire: Definitely goes in the 99 of other decks but easily triggered repeatable blink is great.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Cmdr. Troi, Outgoing Empath

Saffgor: You just know that abbreviation is because they couldn't fit 'Commander', and that's just a little funny. Troi is one of a few different candidate for Izzet politics/group hug, along with Red Death & Itazura, but my main concern is that she might just kingmake a bit too often.

BPhillipYork: This seems potentially really dangerous, but kind of a fun way to play. Obviously you'd really want some way to see into their hand first (which seems like what she should actually do but here we are). Anyway, unpredictable but interesting commander.

FromTheShire: This is super interesting, and a great excuse to play things like Telepathy, Zur's Weirding, and Glasses of Urza. It also means she scales super well to whatever the power level of the table is which I like as well.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Collective Override

Saffgor: Uh...wow, okay, this is about as pushed as a Fog-like can be. This will blow out a lot of opponents, and does a pretty good Jeska's Will impression alongside an Altar/KCI if you're swinging out.

BPhillipYork: Well this seems really good for like, the Borg deck. And potentially good for any kind of go-wide deck, though blue isn't the most common color for go wide, it's definitely viable, especially Esper.

FromTheShire: Sheesh. It doesn't do a full Arachnogenesis or Inkshield unfortunately so most likely the creatures are all dying as chump blockers if you're the one getting attacked, but that's some damn spicy card draw. And if you're the one doing the attacking, or one opponent is attacking another. this becomes an absolute house.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Hugh, First of Many

Saffgor: Replicate is a delightful little additional cost, which means reductions pay for its colorless component. Anything with Affinity for Artifacts is usually able to overflow some of its discount, and in practice have "Replicate {U}", so that's really where Hugh's home is. Great potential here, and while it might not cut it in cEDH you can sure make a ton of Frogmites.

BPhillipYork: That's potentially really nuts. Like it's super expensive, but with cost reduction it gets really cheap suddenly, and you can make a horde or go nuts with mana rocks and triggers (Disciple of the Vault type of thing).

FromTheShire: Fortunate it goes in a deck with lots of cost reducers or else you would never actually be able to pay for the replicate, but once you can it's a banger.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Jurati, Cordial Queen

Saffgor: Token-copy your Artifacts, copy your clones, profit. I wish she had evasion, but I won't turn my nose up at another clone-adjacent Commander that comes in low along the curve.

BPhillipYork: This seems a bit of a win-more type card, but if you build around it, a particularly with some kind of ETB heavy creatures. Using something like Gingerbrute to swing through so you can copy a Sad Robot via a Borg scientist is kind of funny.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Kor, Cause of Vengeance

Saffgor: The fact the Klingon payoffs also state 'Warrior' goes to show why typal strategies in UB that necessitate their own type are doomed to fail. I don't know dude, can we not? There's not enough Klingons, and there's better Warrior Commanders.

BPhillipYork: This isn't all that unique, so it's fine, but not all that exciting. But certainly if you want a Mardu deck around this or just to slot it into a Mardu deck it's fine.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Locutus of Borg

Saffgor: This guy goes exponential, and being in Blue you've got Extra Turns to contend with. Much like crabs, every archetype returns to Edric Flying Men eventually.

BPhillipYork: Well that's potentially a lot of tokens, after a while. Obviously all the Borg work pretty well with each other.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Pavel Chekov, First Posting

Saffgor: Holy shit, Abundance in the Command Zone. Uhh, wow, yeah that's wild to see, and both stops you from ever flooding out...and enables combos. I don't expect him to be popular, but there are some fun '96 Lands and some combo pieces' lists to brew here.

BPhillipYork: This isn't super exciting but you can do things with it or just include it in a deck where you say use a lot of land tutors so you don't ever want to draw land.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu

Saffgor: Killer first ability, and unblockable when you need it helps certain payoffs get in. Give this guy a Banishing Knack and let him go to town with an untap effect.

BPhillipYork: This is fun, a bit expensive, but a nice color combo and it lets you swing through with something you used his explore to ramp to get going.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Command Chair

Saffgor: I think you need at least an 8-mana Commander to make this worthwhile, and that's a fairly slim pool for a 6-mana Artifact. Having to control them as well is another hurdle, so unless you intend to cheat out a Dargo this likely stays in the binder.

BPhillipYork: It's a big mana rock that's really too expensive but some people are into that kind of thing.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Guardian of Forever

Saffgor: A slow Nim Deathmantle of sorts, it's cool to see Colorless have an aristocrats-ish blink-ish Commander now that comes in so low along the curve.

BPhillipYork: Well it's kind of a neat looping sacrifice, really expensive, and also slow, so it's not like you can really abuse it. Though you could use it to avoid removal everyone will see that coming.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

K'Vort-Class Raider

Saffgor: Hexproof like that is nice to see, and given any Commander can play it I expect the Raider to show up, even if it isn't flashy.

BPhillipYork: Well giving creatures your control hexproof during your turn for purely colorless mana is a pretty nice effect to let you do your thing, that seems like that main use of this.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Queen's Diamond

Saffgor: Is this my favorite card in the set? It's certainly close, if I'm to be honest. The Diamond has shades of the now-banned Jeweled Lotus, helping to turbo out Commanders with not too many colors (ideally 2 or fewer) by way of translating power on board into a chunk of restricted mana. This has a much higher ceiling than the Lotus, but a much fairer floor, although the safety it provides to kill-on-sight Commanders or those with obnoxious costs is profound. Heck, it's a pretty good blocker if you don't need to recast your Commander regardless. It might just be the kind of person I am, but every deck I've built post-Star Trek has found room for the Diamond, and that tells me it likely has legs.

BPhillipYork: This is more what I expected a Borg ship to be like, and I like the idea of being able to afford command tax, so nice to see this. It's really something you can include in any color deck having nothing to do with Borg. Having haste and vigilance is also a nice upside so you can just swing away and then use it for mana later. You can also do something crazy with this and Doubling Cube.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

S.S. Botany Bay

Saffgor: Cross off 'Reanimator' from your Colorless Commander archetype list, because this nails that task. A bit of grave hate, a cheap upfront cost, and being in an identity known for its massive beaters. Seems like a slam dunk, if you can actually get the necessary targets in yard.

BPhillipYork: Wow that's a strange but effective reanimator, and also a way to trim your opponents' graveyards when you want. I sort of like the idea of including this as a troll card, that you're just hitting yards with and not really exiling anything and everyone is holding up removal to keep it from reanimating something dangerous.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Starfleet Communicator

Saffgor: Gwyndala use case aside, this is just a ton of draw and ramp if we're being honest. With a pair of attackers suited up, you've basically cast two Growth Spiral on attack, and I'm pretty happy with that. Makes for some genuinely obscene tokens to copy too, as three attackers with these gets out of hand exponentially.

BPhillipYork: This is a more useful communicator, and there's lots of ways to make more copies, which seems like a fun thing. Replicate this with Hugh, First of Many and things can get pretty nuts pretty fast.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Starship Enterprise

Saffgor: This card is attached at the hip to Bant Kirk, and I think its only real use case beyond him is in counter-matters strategies like Maester Seymour & Felisa, Fang of Silverquill. Seems great there though, so who am I to judge? Lovely card.

BPhillipYork: This is one of the stronger spacecraft in my opinion and of course Kirk fetches it which is pretty nice.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Defiant, Mirror Migrant

Saffgor: Fantastic protection piece and a well-overstatted attacker/blocker once Stationed up. This goes in every Commander-reliant strategy you can imagine, and with it being Colorless that's a great number of them. Pick up copies while they're cheap.

BPhillipYork: This is a nice way to save something and then you've got an okay hitter if you want that.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Enterprise-C, Time-Tossed

Saffgor: The only real stellar thing this does is serve as a remarkably funny card to clone. Legend Rule-ing a clone wheels you twice, and that's a stupid amount of discards & draws if there are external payoffs. Not great outside of that.

BPhillipYork: There are some things that care about how many you drew or discarded this turn, and this is a solid way to trigger that a lot, but outside of that I probably wouldn't run this just for pure value in a deck that doesn't specifically leverage what it does.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Farragut, Bold Explorer

Saffgor: I've got a Focus cooking for this one, because giving Colorless access to a Sneak Attack on Landfall is already amazing, and this one even replaces the advantage you'd have otherwise lost. The Farragut, so long as you have enough ramp, is a frighteningly powerful Landfall payoff...and given Landfall requires Lands, which produce mana, you probably have enough ramp to make this spooky.

BPhillipYork: This is fun, especially if you run a ton of ETBs and ramp, it's just ramp into crazy more ramp. It fits well with Kirk and the Enterprise and lots of lands entering and things that fetch lands. Of course it also lets you cheat out huge creatures for a single shot, it's basically Sneak Attack for every color which is insane.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

U.S.S. Prometheus, Prototype

Saffgor: Add 'Voltron' to that Colorless Archetype checklist please. I mean, shoot, this does just kind of do exactly what you want if that's the goal. A hair expensive, but in Bracket 2 you can definitely score some kills.

BPhillipYork: This effect is nice in Commander, if you can pump it you can deal a lot of damage really fast. People will certainly see that coming so you'll want some way to protect it.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Shore Leave Planet

Saffgor: It's weird to print this a set after Hall of Echoes, not going to lie. Feels like some designer miscommunication. If you were playing Hall, play this as well. If you weren't, don't.

BPhillipYork: Copying a creature is nice sometimes, but I don't know that you really want it from lands. It's sort of like a temp clone but it effectively costs you 6, so are you really going to be able to do something if you've already burned through 6 mana?

Next Time: The Set’s White, Blue, & Black Cards

That wraps up our look at the Multicolor and Colorless cards of Star Trek. We’ll be back later this week to continue with the first of the monocolor cards, before wrapping our review up the following week.
