title: All official DnD races and species explained
content:
DnD races represent the different species found in the world's oldest tabletop RPG. Your DnD species (as they've been recently re-named) decides your appearance and culture, but it also determines rules-relevant facts about your size, speed, and abilities.

There are dozens upon dozens of official Dungeons and Dragons races, though the current Player's Handbook features just 10. Whether you want to play a standard species or something rarer, your choice has a big impact on your character. I've painstakingly researched each possible option and explained how they work in this guide.

Before you start shopping for a new species, a few housekeeping rules. D&D 5e now has its own refreshed sub-edition, 5.5e. Some species appear in both, but others don't. I've made it clear where you can find the most up-to-date version of each option. For brevity's sake, I've also only presented the most recent rules - though I've listed other, older sourcebooks you can investigate yourself if you prefer 2014 to 2024.

Also, this isn't my only guide to character creation. I recommend checking out Wargamer's guides to DnD classes and DnD backgrounds, as they complement the character options here pretty well! Okay, now we're ready to begin:

The core DnD races are:

  • Aasimar
  • Dragonborn
  • Dwarf
  • Elf
  • Gnome
  • Goliath
  • Halfling
  • Half-Elf
  • Half-Orc
  • Human
  • Orc
  • Tiefling

All DnD races include:

  • Aasimar
  • Dragonborn
  • Dwarf
  • Elf
  • Gnome
  • Goliath
  • Halfling
  • Half elf
  • Half orc
  • Human
  • Orc
  • Tiefling
  • Aarakocra
  • Astral Elf
  • Autognome
  • Bugbear
  • Centaur
  • Changeling
  • Deep Gnome
  • Dhampir
  • Duergar
  • Duskling
  • Eladrin
  • Fairy
  • Firbolg
  • Genasi
  • Giff
  • Githyanki
  • Githzerai
  • Goblin
  • Hadozee
  • Harengon
  • Hexblood
  • Hobgoblin
  • Kalashtar
  • Kender
  • Kenku
  • Kobold
  • Leonin
  • Lizardfolk
  • Lorwyn Changeling
  • Loxodon
  • Lupin
  • Minotaur
  • Owlin
  • Plasmoid
  • Reborn
  • Rimekin
  • Satyr
  • Sea Elf
  • Shadar kai
  • Shifter
  • Simic Hybrid
  • Tabaxi
  • Thri kreen
  • Tortle
  • Triton
  • Vedalken
  • Verdan
  • Warforged
  • Yuan ti

Aasimar

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forCleric, Warlock, Paladin
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Thanks to a shared ancestry with celestials, each Aasimar is blessed with divine looks and abilities. They're naturally resistant to necrotic and radiant damage, plus they're gifted healers who can roll d4s equal to their proficiency bonus to restore a creature's HP.

All Aasimar can cast the Light cantrip using Charisma as their spellcasting modifier, which implies the optimal builds for this species rely on that stat. However, if you're happy to sacrifice this (very situational) cantrip, an Aasimar can excel in any D&D class.

The Aasimar's most explosive feature is Celestial Revelation. When activated, this can give your Aasimar a fly speed, create a ten-foot emanation of light that deals radiant damage, or force enemies to make a Charisma save or become frightened. Whichever form they take, it lets the Aasimar deal additional radiant or necrotic damage when they attack.

Learn more in our full Aasimar species guide.

Dragonborn

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Strength, +1 Charisma (2014 rules only)
Best forPaladin, Barbarian, Warlock
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Dragonborn resemble humanoid dragons, though D&D lore flip-flops on exactly how this species got its draconic features. However it happened, the Dragonborn's scaly, wingless appearance makes them one of the most recognizable species.

Their signature Breath Weapon helps in that department, too. Able to exhale a force of destructive energy that deals 1d10 damage on a failed Constitution saving throw, they've got an ace in the hole straight out of the gate. Its damage and difficulty class will increase as they level up, and your choice of Draconic Ancestry will determine its damage type, as well as your character's damage resistances.

The Dragonborn also benefits from 60 feet of Darkvision. More excitingly, once they reach level five, they can grow wings as a bonus action to gain a fly speed. We'd recommend this species for martials that usually lack ranged options and mobility.

Learn more in our DnD Dragonborn species guide.

Dwarf

SizeMedium
Speed25ft (2014) or 30ft (2024)
Ability scores+2 Constitution (2014 rules only)
Best forCleric, Fighter, Barbarian, Druid
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Originally members of cave-dwelling clans, the DnD Dwarf species has a reputation for durability and a handy way with stone. Mechanically, this manifests as a resistance to poison damage and advantage on saving throws against being poisoned.

Dwarfs also have the Dwarven Toughness feature, which automatically increases their maximum hit points by one, and it does so again with every DnD level up. It doesn't get much more durable than that. Unsurprisingly, the classes that tend to suit a Dwarf are those looking to keep themselves standing on the front lines of battle.

Beyond this, a Dwarf's skills are defined by their ancient tendency to yearn for the mines. They have extended Darkvision (120ft rather than the standard 60ft) and tremorsense for 60 feet instead of enhanced History rolls when checking out pieces of rock - far more useful, if you ask us.

Learn more in our complete DnD Dwarf guide.

Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Dexterity (2014 rules only)
Best forRogue, Ranger, Wizard, Warlock
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Tall, sleek, and pointy-eared, The DnD Elf is a graceful being, most at home in ethereal forests. Their Darkvision and proficiency in either Insight, Perception, or Survival make them excellent stealthy scouts. Elves also have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and they enter trances instead of going to sleep at night.

Each Elf has an Elven Lineage that decides some of their natural abilities. This makes the Elf an immensely flexible species, perfect for many kinds of characters (though, most of the time, we tend to recommend it for spellcasters).

Drow have enhanced Darkvision, and they can cast Dancing Lights, Faerie Fire, and Darkness. High Elves know Prestidigitation, Detect Magic, and Misty Step - though they can swap the cantrip with another from the Wizard spell list each day. Wood Elves have a base speed of 35 feet, as well as the ability to cast Druidcraft, Longstrider, and Pass Without Trace.

Learn more in our DnD Elf species guide.

Gnome

SizeSmall
Speed25ft (2014) or 30 feet (2024)
Ability scores+2 Intelligence (2014 rules only)
Best forWizard, Rogue, Artificer
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Vibrant and expressive, DnD Gnomes are often styled as a curious and cunning race that enjoys the thrill of adventure. However you choose to roleplay them, all Gnomes gain the same basic benefits - Darkvision, plus advantage on all Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws.

When you decide to play a Gnome, you'll choose a specific Gnomish Lineage. Forest Gnomes are illusionists who can speak to small beasts (often without wasting a spell slot). Meanwhile, Rock Gnomes can cast Mending and Prestidigitation, and they can still tinker with tools to create a small mechanical device.

A species that gains extra spells is usually a surefire pick for a spellcasting class, as it beefs up their existing repertoire. The Rogue is our wildcard suggestion, though. Gnomes are great at finding non-violent solutions to problems, which pairs well with the Rogue's utility-focused approach.

Learn more about this species in our DnD Gnome guide.

Goliath

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet (2014) or 35 feet (2024)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

A DnD Goliath may only be slightly bigger than your average human, but they have strength that rivals their Giant ancestors. They're as durable as granite, and they make for great martial characters.

The Goliath has advantage on checks against the grappled condition, and from level five onwards, they can become Large for 10 minutes, which gives them advantage on Strength checks and increases their speed by 10 feet, as well as greatly enlarging the area they affect in combat. Hulk, smash!

Additionally, the Goliath chooses one ability that's unique to their Giant Ancestry. This might allow them to teleport as a bonus action, deal extra damage, slow or knock enemies prone, or even reduce the damage the Goliath takes. Giant Ancestry is so versatile that you could play six or seven Goliaths and not have one feel same-y.

Learn more in our DnD Goliath guide.

Halfling

SizeSmall
Speed25ft (2014) or 30ft (2024)
Ability scores+2 Dexterity (2014 rules only)
Best forRogue, Ranger, Bard
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

Halflings are almost identical to the Hobbits of Tolkien's Middle-earth, though without the thick foot hair and round front doors. Living in peaceful, bucolic communities usually hidden from the conflicts of the world, they're cheerful and curious.

Halflings are extra nimble, able to move through the space of any creature that's at least one DnD size larger than them. They're also brave, with advantage on saves against the frightened condition, and lucky, meaning they're able to reroll any 1 on a d20. As well as luck and courage, Halflings have stealth to fall back on, as they can Hide as long as they're obscured by a creature at least one size larger than them.

All kinds of characters benefit from extra luck, but we tend to build Halfling characters that get maximum value from their stealth and mobility. That means Scout characters and anyone who needs an easy way to escape mid-fight.

For a full description, check out our DnD Halfling guide.

Half-Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 any other stat (2014 rules only)
Best forBard, Sorcerer
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2014)

Born of Human and Elf parents, DnDHalf-Elf characters take bits from both of their ancestral lines. Thanks to their Elf lineage, they have Darkvision and are immune to being put to sleep. They also have the versatility of Humans, which gives them proficiency in two extra DnD skills.

Like Elves, Half-Elves have a subrace that can give them further powers. However, if you want to take the optional features of a Drow, High, or Wood Half-Elf, you must sacrifice the extra skill proficiencies granted by your Human ancestry. In their place, you can learn additional spells, become trained in additional weapons, or gain a swimming speed.

Species of dual parentage like the Half-Elf and the Half-Orc (who we'll discuss in a moment) weren't included in the 2024 Player's Handbook, so you'll only have the 2014 version to work with. Still, their flexible DnD stats and skills make them strong Charisma casters. The Bard is our top choice of class for the species overall.

Want to learn more? Here's our full DnD Half-Elf species guide.

Half-Orc

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Strength, +1 Constitution (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2014)

With Orc and Human blood running through their veins, Half-Orcs partially resemble the classic Tolkien-esque creatures. They're physically mighty, and they may have visible teeth and green-ish skin.

Their famed physical might is realized through their Relentless Endurance and Savage Attacks. The first ability means that, should a Half-Orc be downed in battle, they can immediately bounce back with one HP. Savage Attack, meanwhile, lets them roll an additional attack die whenever they land a critical hit - perfect for massive bursts of damage.

Like the Half-Elf, the Half-Orc was left out of the 2024 rules update. However, you can still shoehorn them into your games thanks to backwards compatibility. Whether you use their associated ability score increase or not, Half-Orcs are best suited to melee-based martial classes.

Here's a complete guide to the DnD Half-Orc that can tell you more.

Human

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 in all stats, or +1 in two stats plus a feat and skill (2014 rules only)
Best forAll
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Player's Handbook (2014)

DnD Human characters are variable and adaptable folks, who ambitiously explore the land for both personal gain and altruistic devotion. Their lives are short, but their empires are enormous.

Humans are by far the most versatile of the common species. The 2014 version gives you complete control over your ability score increases, and the popular Variant Human gains a feat for free straight out of the gate.

In the 2024 rules, every character gains a free DnD 2024 feat at level one, but the Human can choose a second feat. They also start with an extra skill proficiency, and they gain Inspiration whenever they finish a long rest. Whichever version of the Human you're planning to use, they're an excellent choice for basically any class.

Learn more in our DnD Human species guide.

Orc

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two stats or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forPaladin, Cleric, Fighter
SourcebookPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

While they're stereotyped as villains in a lot of fantasy media (including past editions of D&D), the Orc 5e has as much right to be a heroic adventurer as anyone else. The Half-Orc's large teeth, green skin, and physical might are all inherited from this species.

An Orc is best known for their imposing strength. Like the Half-Orc, this is represented by the Relentless Endurance ability, which lets them drop to one hit point instead of zero if they are downed in combat. Additionally, Adrenaline Rush lets them dash as a bonus action, Rogue-style, and it gives the Orc temporary HP equal to their proficiency bonus.

Orcs are a natural choice for Strength-based martial builds, though always going for Strength-based builds might start to feel a bit same-y after a while. If you want to shake it up, any fragile spellcaster would appreciate abilities that help them to avoid death.

Tiefling

SizeMedium or Small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 Intelligence (2014 rules only)
Best forWarlock, Sorcerer, Wizard
SourcebooksPlayer's Handbook (2024); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018); Player's Handbook (2014)

Tieflings have a unique appearance, thanks to their horns, tails, and vibrantly colored skin. These traits come from their ancestry, as somewhere along the line a devil, demon, or yugoloth joined or afflicted their family. This heritage also provides them with resistance to certain DnD damage types and extra spellcasting abilities.

While there are a vast number of Tiefling variants in D&D's many books, the 2024 variant of 5e presents three. Abyssal Tieflings are resistant to poison damage, and they learn Poison Spray, Ray of Sickness, and Hold Person. Chthonic Tieflings are resistant to necrotic damage, and they learn Chill Touch, False Life, and Ray of Enfeeblement. Finally, Infernal Tieflings have fire resistance, and they'll learn Fire Bolt, Hellish Rebuke, and Darkness.

Best forDruid, Cleric
SourcebooksGuildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

Hailing from the Magic: The Gathering plane of Ravnica, the Loxodon 5e is a humanoid-elephant species known for its powerful trunk. Said trunks can be used to lift items and interact with objects, which is extra-impressive thanks to the Loxodon's heightened carrying capacity.

Perhaps more excitingly, this trunk can also make unarmed strikes in combat. Combine this with the Loxodon's natural armor of 12 + their Constitution modifier, and you've got a hardy wisdom caster.

The Loxodon's advantage on Perception, Survival, and Investigation checks mean they're also capable scouts. The Druid is our top class pick here, but Cleric and Ranger make just as much sense.

Lupin

SizeMedium or Small
Speed30 feet
Ability scoresN/A
Best forMonk
SourcebooksRavenloft: The Horrors Within (2026)

Half-wolf, half-another-species hybrids, Lupins are like werewolves who got stuck halfway through their transformation in that awkward wolf-person stage. It's not a bad shape for adventuring in, though.

Lupins get Darkvision out to 60 feet, have improved Unarmed Strikes thanks to those slashing talons, and can let out a terrifying and disorienting howl. Their werewolf instincts also make them proficient in Perception, Stealth, or Survival.

The Lupin's ability to deal damage and shove enemies with the same unarmed strike is going to synergise best with the Monk - but it's a small buff that you could choose to overlook. The strength of their howl depends on Constitution, which every class benefits from improving.

Minotaur

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Guildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

The Minotaur 5e race is said to hail from the deadly mazes of the Planescape setting. Supposedly tasked with patrolling the magical mazes of the Lady of Pain, Minotaurs have developed an excellent sense of direction - as well as some handy combat skills. While there's some scout potential, most of the Minotaur's abilities focus on brute strength.

Labyrinthine Recall gives your character advantage on any Survival check when navigating or tracking. A Minotaur can also use their horns to make unarmed strikes that deal 1d6 plus their Strength modifier in piercing damage. Plus, Goring Rush allows you to make a Horns attack as a bonus action if you Dash for at least 20 feet.

Alternatively, your Minotaur could use Hammering Horns. After a successful melee attack, this ability lets you push the target with your horns as a bonus action. As long as they're within five feet, aren't more than one size larger than you, and don't succeed on a Strength saving throw, your target is pushed ten feet away.

Owlin

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft (walking and flying)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRogue, Ranger
SourcebooksStrixhaven: A Curriculum of Chaos (2021)

An Owlin 5e is, as the name implies, a humanoid that resembles a fluffy, wise owl. Such avian lineage has plenty of perks, including twice the Darkvision most species have, as well as automatic proficiency in stealth. Combine this with the power of flight, and you've got a character that can swoop in silence, swiftly taking out foes.

These traits make the Owlin a great pick for a Ranger or a Rogue. Their flexible ability scores mean you could choose Owlins for any build, but we don't think a Barbarian will have quite the same amount of fun with those racial traits. Plus, their flight prevents them from wearing most armor, so beefier frontliners won't be able to enjoy both wings and full plate.

Check out our full Owlin 5e guide to learn more.

Plasmoid

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forMonk
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The Plasmoid 5e is as close as it gets to playing a Gelatinous Cube. These sentient piles of goo stand out from the crowd thanks to their ability to shapeshift with ease. The Amorphous ability lets them squeeze through any space at least one inch wide - impressive.

The downside is that you can't wear or carry anything while squeezing through that space. The armorless DnD Monk 5e is a natural choice, and they can also benefit from the Plasmoid's advantage on grapple checks.

Even better, a Plasmoid can excrete psuedopods that can manipulate objects for you from a distance. That's a scouting ability that, while it might unsettle your party, will certainly be useful to your allies.

Reborn

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three (2014 rules only)
Best forBarbarian, Bard Rogue
SourcebooksRavenloft: The Horrors Within

A Reborn is a humanoid of a different species that died and, against all odds, returned to life. Their new physical form bears some mark of this event - perhaps a ghostly glow, stitches from being pieced back together, or skeletal limbs. Most Reborn have also lost the memories of their past life.

Your character doesn't need to eat, drink, sleep, or breathe, and can't gain Exhaustion levels those ways, and they have advantage on death saving throws. They're also resistant to poison, cold, or necrotic damage and have advantage on saves against disease or the poisoned condition. Plus, they can finish a long rest in four hours and occasionally add a d6 to their skill checks - thanks, corpse-like body and missing memories!

The version of this species originally printed in 2021's 'Van Richten's Guide to Ravenloft' was a lineage rather than a race, which took a few minor details (skill proficiencies and unusual speeds, for example) from another DnD race. Everything else is Reborn rules, though.

Learn more in our Reborn 5e guide.

Rimekin

SizeMedium or Small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forSorcerer, Warlock
SourcebooksLorwyn: First Light (2025)

Lorwyn's Rimekin are humanoids surrounded by icy cold magic. In D&D terms, that doesn't give you much to get excited about. You have Darkvision and resistance to cold damage, sure, but your only other perk is access to a smattering of Cold Fire Magic.

That means having Ray of Frost on your resume, followed by Ice Knife and Flame Blade at levels three and five. These spells are painfully fine, and they're not likely to revolutionize a build. Still, if you love the chilly flavor of a Rimekin, I'd recommend pairing them with a spellcaster in need of a few extra tricks.

Satyr

SizeMedium
Speed35ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forBard, Paladin
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Mythic Odysseys of Theros (2020)

The whimsical, goat-like Satyr 5e have their origins in the Feywild, and they're full Fey creatures rather than humanoids. Their natural proficiency with Performance, Persuasion, and a musical instrument may make them seem like natural Bards. However, the Satyr's other abilities suit a range of builds.

Magic Resistance grants advantage on saving throws against spells, which is handy for anyone battling a mage. Satyrs also have maneuverability and martial power, as their Satyr's Ram feature deals 1d6 plus their Strength modifier in bludgeoning damage. Plus, they can make Mirthful Leaps, extending their jump distance by their Strength stat.

Neither are game-breaking abilities, but if you want to make use of them, we'd recommend playing a Paladin. Extra movement and an always-available melee attack are pretty decent backup plans.

Sea Elf

SizeMedium
Speed30ft (swimming and walking)
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Cleric
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018)

A Sea Elf 5e is, yes, an Elf that can swim fast and breathe underwater. They're the Aquamen of the Forgotten Realms, able to communicate with swimming beasts and resistant to cold damage.

This water-dwelling humanoid is like its land-based brethren in many ways. Mechanically, we're talking about Darkvision, advantage on rolls against being charmed, and the ability to go into a trance rather than sleep.

While Sea Elves are particularly perceptive and can swap weapon proficiencies on a regular basis, they don't offer many unique abilities. Unless you're part of an adventure that takes place in or under water, there aren't too many advantages to choosing this species.

Shadar-kai

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes (2018)

The Shadar-kai 5e is a species of Elf native to the Shadowfell. Their appearance and abilities have been altered by life in this grim and dark plane, and many of them pledge service to its most powerful deity, The Raven Queen.

In fact, all Shadar-kai have the Blessing of the Raven Queen, an ability that allows them to teleport as a bonus action. After level three, this even grants the Shadar-kai resistance to all damage types for a turn.

As creatures of the night, they're also naturally resistant to necrotic damage and able to see in the dark. And because they're Elves they share many species benefits with their cousins - trance resting, keen senses, fey ancestry, and so on.

Fully customizable ability score increases, plus several free teleports per long rest, mean that the Shadar-kai is an excellent option for any class. If you want to fully optimize, aim for a class that can't already cast Misty Step but would benefit from hopping in and out of melee range.

Shifter

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores-
Best forBarbarian, Fighter
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Eberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

The Shifter 5e race is often called the 'weretouched' thanks to their lycanthrope ancestors. Since they're only part were-beast, they still have a humanoid appearance, but perhaps with a slightly more bestial look. However, they can also partially transform into a werewolf-like form, giving them some formidable battle abilities.

Their Shifting ability gives this species one of several beastly forms, which come with one of four different abilities. Big beastly shifters get Beasthide, granting temporary hit points and a +1 to the Shifter's armor class.

The other options are Longtooth, giving an unarmed fang attack, Swiftstride, granting extra speed and letting you move without triggering opportunity attacks when an enemy stops five feet from you, and Wildhunt, which gives an advantage on Wisdom checks and prevents close-up attacks against you being made with advantage.

Plenty of these powers would benefit a canny martial character, but I can also picture a caster using Swiftstride to get out of trouble.

Simic Hybrid

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Constitution, +1 any other stat
Best forBarbarian, Monk
SourcebooksGuildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

A Simic Hybrid 5e is a humanoid who has been infused with the traits of animals (usually amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, or fish) transforming them into a unique species. Apart from Darkvision, Simic Hybrids only gain one species feature, but they manage to do a lot with it.

All Simic Hybrids start play with either: a climbing speed; a swimming speed and the ability to breathe underwater; or the power to sprout fins that can glide and reduce fall damage. Later, at level five, these characters can choose a different option from this list - or they can pick from a pile of new powers.

This includes basic bonuses like a +1 to your armor class, as well as some more elaborate options. Some Simic Hybrids can spray acid as an action, with the 2d10 damage dealt increasing as they gain level ups.

Others can grow two entirely new appendages, which are perfect for making unarmed strikes and grapples as a bonus action. This used to make the species perfect for Monks, but the 2024 version of the class can perform these feats anyway - so we'd stick to builds that have less to do with their bonus actions.

Tabaxi

SizeMedium
Speed30ft walking and climbing
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forRogue, Monk
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

All Tabaxi were created by the feline Cat Lord, but two of them are rarely alike. Despite the huge variation in appearances and abilities, there are two things that all Tabaxi excel in - agility and stealth.

For example, all Tabaxi have the power to move double their usual speed on a turn (though they'll need to spend a turn standing still to restore that power). Their cat-like claws offer an alternative unarmed attack method, dealing 1d6 plus their Strength modifier in damage.

Plus, these cunning cats all have proficiency in Perception and Stealth. Combine this with 30 feet of climbing speed, and you've got an excellent species for Scout characters.

Check out our Tabaxi 5e species guide for more details. 

Thri-kreen

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forRanger, Rogue, Fighter
SourcebooksSpelljammer: Adventures in Space (2022)

The Thri-kreen 5e is a giant space bug with four arms and telepathic powers. That's a concept that's bound to inspire plenty of interesting D&D characters. Plus, thanks to the Thri-kreen's funky arms, they have a lot of potential for interesting character builds.

Your Secondary Arms ability lets you use your two smaller arms to manipulate objects, interact with doors and containers, pick up tiny objects, or wield light weapons. That last one is key - you can now wield weapons and shields with hands left over for spellcasting, extra weapons, and so on.

Tortle

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+1 and +2 any two, or +1 any three
Best forDruid, Ranger
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Explorer's Guide to Wildemount (2020); The Tortle Package (2017)

The Tortle 5e race may look like a tortoise, but there's nothing slow or dull about them. They're a particularly hardy species, with a natural armor class of 17 (though they can't wear regular armor). A Tortle gains even more defensive power from their signature shell, which they can retreat into to gain advantage on Strength and Constitution rolls.

Tortles can choose from plenty of Wisdom-based and Scout-friendly skill proficiencies. Combine this with their extra defenses, and you've got a species that can make your standard Druid or Ranger build far more durable.

To learn more, check out our DnD Tortle 5e guide.

Triton

SizeMedium
Speed30ft walking, 30ft swimming
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2018)

If you're playing a sea-faring campaign, the Triton 5e is a handy ally to have. Their Amphibious nature means they can breathe air and water, and Emissary of the Sea lets them share basic ideas with creatures that have a swimming speed.

Most of the Triton's unique features offer basic utility. Darkvision is always nice to have, and Guardian of the Depths grants resistance to cold damage. Plus, thanks to Control Air and Water, you can cast Fog Cloud, Gust of Wind, and Water Walk (spell slots optional).

These spells aren't going to break any character builds, and they don't push the Triton towards any particular class. If you're planning to play a Triton, you're probably not planning to power-build anyway - so pick the class that calls to your water-loving heart.

Vedalken

SizeMedium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Intelligence, +1 Wisdom
Best forWizard, Artificer
SourcebooksGuildmaster's Guide to Ravnica (2018)

Vedalken 5e are partially amphibious creatures who, apart from their blue skin and lack of hair, closely resemble tall humans. Their most powerful ability isn't particularly flavorful, but it has an explosive mechanical effect. Vedalken have advantage on all Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma saving throws, meaning they're particularly well-defended against magical effects.

Vedalken can also breathe underwater for up to one hour (once per long rest), but this ability pales in comparison with that first trait. Protection against magic is a buff for pretty much any D&D character, after all.

If you need help narrowing down your choices, look to the Vedalken's proficiencies for suggestions. The species is proficient in an extra tool, plus one skill from this list: Arcana, History, Investigation, Medicine, Performance, and Sleight of Hand. This implies a slight advantage for Intelligence-based casters and skill-focused characters - though a Vedalken Barbarian is still perfectly viable.

Verdan

SizeSmall or medium
Speed30 feet
Ability scores+2 Charisma, +1 Constitution
Best forSorcerer, Warlock, Bard
SourcebooksAcquisitions Incorporated (2019)

Introduced by Acquisitions Incorporated, the Verdan 5e evolved from goblinoids, though they're often confused for Half-Elves. Whatever their origin, they're best known for their ability to speak telepathically with any creature they can see within 30 feet.

Verdan are also proficient in Persuasion, as well as Wisdom and Charisma saving throws. They're an excellent choice for Charisma casters, though many characters could take advantage of that extra protection against spells.

We'd recommend choosing the Verdan if your preferred class is a bit squishy. Their Black Blood Healing ability allows them to reroll a 1 or 2 on a Hit Dice roll, which will help keep you on your feet between fights.

Warforged

SizeMedium
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 Constitution, +1 one other score
Best forArtificer, Barbarian, Cleric
SourcebooksEberron: Rising from the Last War (2019)

Members of the Warforged 5e race were once mindless automaton soldiers in the DnD setting of Eberron, but at some point, they gained sentience. Now they're ready to join an adventuring party, armed with their newfound emotions and an artificial body that's ideal for soaking up damage.

Warforged don't need to do pesky mortal things like eat, drink, breathe, or sleep, but they do require rest and healing like any other humanoid. Being made of wood and metal, they're less affected by poisons and they're blessed with a boosted armor class. They can also meld their DnD armor of choice to their body so enemies can't remove it.

To learn more about the Warforged 5e, here's our full guide to the species. 

Yuan-ti

SizeMedium or small
Speed30ft
Ability scores+2 and +1 two different stats, or +1 any three
Best forAny
SourcebooksMordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse (2022); Volo's Guide to Monsters (2016)

Part human and part snake, the Yuan-ti 5e can often be distinguished by their serpent eyes, noses, or tongues. These snake-like features come with plenty of perks, including Darkvision, resistance to poison damage, and advantage on rolls against the poisoned condition.

Yuan-ti also gain serpentine spellcasting powers, meaning they can cast Poison Spray, Suggestion, and Animal Friendship (though that last one only works on snakes).

Any adventurer can benefit from the Yuan-ti's handy resistances, but these species traits are a little underwhelming, and none lend themselves well to a particular class. If we were going purely on flavor, we'd make a Swarmkeeper Ranger who can summon an army of slithering friends.

Got a D&D character in mind already? Here are the best DnD campaigns and DnD one shots you could play them in. We can also recommend some other tabletop RPGs to try if you want to go beyond D&D.

title: MTG Star Trek boxes plummet on the secondary market
content:
MTG Star Trek products are tanking in price, with play booster boxes selling for $107 on TCGPlayer one day before the set's official global launch date. That's just $3.57 per pack - about half their $6.99 MSRP. While low prerelease reports are just anecdotal evidence, this is a strong sign that - at least at this early stage, fans aren't biting on this release.

Things aren't, perhaps, quite as dire as they might sound from that description. No one pays the 'per pack' value for a play booster box on release - not even for a banger set like Final Fantasy. In truth, it wouldn't be surprising to see the box selling for about $120 right now.

However, $107 is a fair bit lower than that, and it makes Star Trek the most affordable Universes Beyond set upon launch in the last year, behind Marvel Super Heroes ($121), TMNT ($123.50), and Avatar The Last Airbender ($150).

At the same time as this Universes Beyond product seems to be tanking, another release all about obscure references to MTG lore is doing exceptionally well.

Commander Mystery Booster has an MSRP value of $250, but it's already selling for a whopping $450 on the secondary market. This may have as much to do with a limited supply than the demand. The preorders on the Secret Lair website sold out within minutes, and fans are clamouring for this product.

While Mystery Booster: Commander edition will be available in some numbers at MagicCon Atlanta, I doubt very much that there'll be enough boxes available to make a significant dent in that price tag.

If you like our articles, why not come join our Discord. Are you looking forward to MagicCon? We've got our eyes peeled for the Nauctis previews - should be a breath of fresh air.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Adeptus Custodes Legends Datasheets
content:
With the release of the Adeptus Custodes Codex, we've also seen what was left of the old Forgeworld Upgrade Kits, Aleya/Valerian along with the Land Raider, and Venerable Contemptor sent to the annals of Legends. Unfortunate to see most of these go, especially when Sisters of Silence lack a proper Leader character and the Custodes Units that did go benefit so much from the new Codex.

But that said, these units do still have a place at narrative games, casual play, and... are unusually well designed and appear to have some foresight put into them.

I'll break this down by categories, saving the best for last.

Vehicles

Venerable Land Raider

A theme I've noticed with a lot of these datasheets is "The Legends get the last laugh," as they have tools a lot of Custodes lists will want. For example, D3+3 Damage anti-tank weapons, ranged firepower in general, and a solid transport. It's annoying that it did not get a second ability like so many of the other Land Raiders in the Space Marine Codex, but the assault disembark is something a lot of Custodes lists want; a way to safely carry a couple of squads of troops is huge. The issue, however, is this will become the ultimate priority target on the field. The transport capacity of 6 means Leaders in their squads put this unit in a very awkward position. As you'll either have two empty seats, or just shove a couple squads of Terminators/Custodian Guard, etc. (This also adds a very hilarious option of just shoving a little under two-thirds of your entire list into a single transport by putting two Blade Champions, one Shield Captain, one Allarus Shield Captain, Trajann, and Valerian into a single transport. Don't do this unless you're going for a really insane narrative mission.) Also, it's well-pointed at 230. Very good decision to go lower since Custodes appear to have launched overcosted.

Venerable Contemptor Dreadnought

Lots of small improvements on the old VenCon that keep it a pretty decent choice in the right match-up. Keeping the normal upgrades from the other Contemptor Pattern dreadnoughts like the Achillus/Galatus, the VenCon went to M9, T10, 2+/4++ (WHOA BABY!) Kheres Pattern Assault Cannon is now AP-2, Damage 2, even has Sustained Hits 1 built in (and it is not conditional; it just works against everything!), and it's a good Strength 7. I could see this being absolutely devastating in Might of the Morotoi and Aquilan Shield, as it can get a lot out of these detachments, rerolls from Might, fallback shoot, and charge, along with +1S from Aquilan Shield. Also, in a nice change of pace and consistency, the Contemptor Fist has been upped to AP-3 D3+3 damage, matching the Redemptor/Brutalis Fists, meaning it can punch up and hit about as hard as it's Marine Contemporaries. The Unyielding Ancient ability to bring back has been nerfed, but it trades the potential extra wounds for consistency in that you'll always get back up with 3W, not great, but it could be a lot worse... Maybe. Currently pointed at 220 points, it's a good beasty; it can help if you need something to fight infantry or bully Space Marines in general.

Credit: Jack Hunter

Infantry

Custodian Guard Sodality with Adrasite Spears

What a GLOW UP on the Gun. 2 shots a piece, now S8 AP-2 and 3D; that's just nasty. Combo this with Aquilan Shield for the fallback shoot and charge, and now the new unit has the ability to reroll wounds of 1 or reroll all wounds on an objective. (Note: You don't have to control it either.) Extra shots were badly needed, but going from S5 to S8 means you have a unit that can punch up HARD now. You've got dedicated Terminator hunters with all this 3D, and even take the fight to vehicles with the fishing via full wound rerolls. You can even put the fear of the Emperor in a Custodes Mirror Match with the +1S from Aquilan Shield so you can punch into even Allarus Terminators, or annoy all those Space Marine Land Speeders, or some of the smaller Daemon Engines and Tau Vehicles with this. Also 200 points for 3. That's amazing, a full 40-point drop from rank-and-file Custodian Guard and even better is they still get the Trusted Sentinel keyword, so the unit benefits from the new rules from Honoured Companions and Guardians of the Throne, immensely, along with Salvus Stance ignoring those silly things like cover.

Custodian Guard Sodality with Pyrithite Spears

Now we get to something beautiful, an infantry anti-tank weapon. Still only one shot, but was raised to match a lot of the other Melta Weapon profiles at S10 and AP-3 with D3+2 Damage, but the big winner is if you run Aquilan Shield and pop +6" range so even coming in relatively safe can still get you the Melta Damage Boost, what's more while the unit keeps the old 10E ability of getting Lethal Hits and Ignores Cover Once Per Battle, they also are Trusted Sentinels which means you can take Honoured Companions and give the squad wound-rerolls of 1. Then it gets even better: there's a reason to run a Pyrithite Spear Captain beyond just the -1 Damage shield. 4 Melta Shots with wound rerolls and potentially much more depending on detachment choice means that this unit has an immense amount of flexibility. Also, 215 points for 3 is great for Custodian Units and especially infantry. After testing this unit, my advice is using this to fight things you don't want to immediately charge; rapid ingress your Captain and Pyrithite Guard somewhere safe, jump out next turn and melta blast, if the target isn't dead? Charge in and finish the job!

But the big winner of the Infantry? Oh, here we go!

Sagittarum Guard by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Sagittarum Custodians Sodality Squad

Try saying that three times fast! Gone but never forgotten, you glorious Rifleman Custodes! (I hope for a resculpt!) And what a glow-up these boys have gotten. Gone are their rifles being a sad mess of AP-1 and situational buffs. No, now they fight like true Gunstodes! Flat Sustained Hits 1 is already great, but now a statline of 3A S7 AP-2 2D and are only 185 points per 3?! W H A T?! This is glorious! I could see narrative lists fielding a lot of these units as backline gun support, slapping on the unit's Debuff of the suppression -1 to hit left and right while filling in awkward holes in the game, and yet again, someone was awake when they wrote this unit and made sure to give the Trusted Sentinel keyword to the unit, so now the unit can reroll wounds of 1 if you take Honoured Companions, pop this with the Once Per Game Devastating Wounds? You can really bring the hurt if you need it. Awesome work all around.

Characters

Aleya

Aleya is basically unchanged except gaining Scouts... 6"? Why? Every other unit scouts 7" that can for the Sisters of Silence. Also, for some reason, she missed the memo, as Somnus still has regular Devastating Wounds. Aleya's unit ability is the same; it has the same keywords, mostly. I advise taking her if you want to throw down a surgical strike assault of the Vigilators; otherwise, don't really bother. However, Aleya is priced at 55 points, so if you're one of the dozen or so Sisters of Silence fans that own enough to make the idea work, Aleya's a great take as she hits hard and moves quickly; her ability is unchanged from 10th edition, right down to the "+1 to wound when below half strength" part that always stings. Then there's the funny thing with Aleya: she's a Leader, and the Knight-Centura is a Support, so you could have a giant 12 model blob consisting of Aleya, a Knight-Centura, and 10 Vigilators all riding out from an Anathema Psykana Rhino. Pretty cheap mid-board skirmisher combo, all things considered.

Credit: Daniel "Skails" Rodenberg

Valerian

(BROKEN COMBO WARNING! BROKEN COMBO WARNING! ABANDON ALL HOPE YE WHO FIELD THIS COMBO!) Are you nostalgic for the days when armor saves were an all-or-nothing situation? Do you long for the days of 7th edition, when AP was more a suggestion to Custodes, and nothing ever died? Do you crave to see your chosen squad caked in the only material more durable than Aurumite, or a named character without a helmet, as they stride across an open battlefield soaking up insane amounts of damage? Well then, you need Valerian and a squad of Wardens! Because whoever was writing the Legends rules did not get the giant slip of paper saying WARDENS HAVE ALWAYS ON ARMOUR OF CONTEMPT! Now Valerian has always-active Armour of Contempt! I hoped you enjoyed it, folks, but we're too late now! We now have a four Custodian-sized, unkillable mob that refuses to die to conventional firearms, and even makes Melta Weapons struggle! Unlike most of the other units, this combo in particular wants to go into Guardians of the Throne. How does ignoring all AP-2 or lower weapons, with -1 to hit and wound via Shield of Honour, sound? Because to me I punch that into my Mathhammer and it makes a happy face! Oh, wait, someone's shooting Ap-3 or 4 weapons at you? Yeah, pop In Auramite Clad! Here, let's just ignore all AP-3! It'll be fine!" [Additional warning: Valerian and Wardens is a combo that should be used cautiously, as this unit is punishing as can be and warrants a careful response from the opponent that not all players can counteract. Use this combo respectfully, if someone in your Crusade Campaign is being a power-gaming maniac, or you really, really, really REALLY HATE your opponent.]

Final Thoughts

To summate: Custodes have some amazing legends units that deserve your attention and consideration, the combos the infantry alone have potential here are worth everyone's attention and for narrative, casual play, and anything else? It's a good sign. I also hope that with how well build so much of this is, it's a sign of a possible resculpt for the fancy spears and the Saagitarum Custodes. (LET ME HUFF MY COPIUM!) None of these besides Valerian are broken, they're just good, and in the world of 40K, especially in Narrative play? Good, is fantastic. I hope this is the standard a lot of Legends rules are in the future.

Overall rating, A-.

title: Mayday, Miss Marcy! 11th Edition, Holiday Hobby, Storage Wars
content:
Hello everyone and welcome back to Mayday, Miss Marcy!, in which I take your reader submitted questions and provide them with the best advice I can come up with in response, which is generally helpful (I like to think, at least). If you're new to the column, think of the likes of Dear Abby or any Agony Aunt style work. The weather sure is cooling down in most places above the Equator, and with that comes the ever encroaching holiday season. Surprisingly, this week I do NOT have any questions about gift giving, but I'm sure there'll be more! If you'd like to have your own questions submitted to the column, please read the blurb below.

Have a question you want answered on just about anything you’d need advice on in this grand hobby space of ours? Board games, 40k, AOS, TTRPGs, MTG, anything and everything that we cover, we can help with!

For some examples, take a look at previous editions of our column at this link with a handy tag to see all previous questions and answers!

If you want to submit questions, we have a few ways you can do it. Patrons can use the Discord bot command to ask questions, which will be received anonymously!

If you’re not a Patron, or just don’t want extra steps, you can comment on this article, or e-mail me directly at marcy@tabletopbattles.com!

As I mentioned, we've been having a collection of gift related questions, and if you haven't had the chance to read last week's column, go take a look! This week, I have a collection of three new questions, so let's get right into them!

New Edition, Old Problem

Hey again Marcy!

Since sending my original question my organizational skills have improved and what was quite a cumbersome collection has been compacted quite a bit! But today is a 40k question.
I'm the local TO for my town, we run small RTTs and other events, but i've came into a bit of a problem; I think the game sort of stinks right now. That is not to say playing 40k is bad, but I feel like matched play is in a woefully boring state, and will not be getting better any time soon. This is a fixable issue, but it may be a couple years before that even happens (the primary mission/dispositions being the bugbear).
So as a TO, where do I go with this? I see two main routes ahead. I could thug it out and keep providing matched play for an admittedly dwindling audience who VERY vocally prefer it, or I can scrap it and go all in on narrative and campaigns, which may alienate some players but save my sanity.
Which direction should I go, or is there a secret third way i'm not seeing?
Regards,
Cluttered Canuck
Dear Canuck,
Thanks for writing in again! Glad to hear from you. I unfortunately think that you're seeing what a lot of people are feeling, and something that even we've seen in the Discord and on various places; while there is some really cool stuff in 11th and obviously a lot of things we haven't seen yet, it does seem like a sense of fatigue has set in over the game already. I'm sure more competent players than I could expand upon why that is, but the reality is that the reason doesn't matter as much as other aspects do, because while GW may be the one to solve the problem, that also means those of us playing the game until then have to figure out how to do so.
I think that your solution is the latter; you should start trying to run different events and seeing if that helps stir the pot on interest levels. If you're having a problem with attendance already, continuing forward is unlikely to make that number go back up, and until something more concrete shows up that gets your locals interested again, trying something new is probably the best way to solve the problem in the short term. Even if you don't run the campaigns forever, spicing up the routine is going to probably at least drag some people back in who have otherwise found issues with wanting to be motivated in the first place.
I think that the lack of narrative and crusade in particular has likely created some issues also; although the gameplay itself is good, if people aren't having fun and don't feel invested, it becomes harder to convince them to keep playing. If you can invent some narrative missions and concepts yourself, it might help to then spur on more play and interest. Although, even though people seem to believe "narrative" = "casual", I think we all know that isn't true, but it DOES tend to bring people to the table. I think you've got the right idea, and just have to work on making it until something else takes the weight off of you; perhaps we'll get some update to 11th that helps bring people back, but you've still got to run your tables! Good luck out there and let us know how it goes, cause I think many people are asking the same questions.

Holiday Hustle

Dear Miss Marcy,

During the holidays, things tend to be busy around our household. In the last year, I realized that I haven't had much time to myself during them, which also meant that my hobby progress basically ground to a complete halt. I'm not thrilled by this, even if it sounds selfish. My hobby is the thing I do for myself and my stress relief / reward for putting up with work, and while I love the holidays and doing things with my family, I absolutely realized that last year I had a few moments where the lack of "me time" was really spreading me thin.

This year I've decided that I want to avoid this from happening, but I'm kind of struggling with how to go about it. Do I just tell my partner "hey, I'm going to go paint some miniatures now" or something while relatives are around or plans are being made? I feel like there's a wrong answer and a right answer; do I just have to accept that my hobby time isn't really "mine" during a busy season like the holidays?

Hobbyist Hangups

Dear Hobbyist,

I... think you know the answer to this, don't you?

If I can be honest, your question does come across as selfish, but for a few reasons that are different than you might expect: You talk a lot about yourself and how the holidays encroach on your "me" time, but you don't really illustrate something. Does your partner get their me time? What about your family in general? Are you the only person doing literally everything while others rest, or are you just looking for your own peace of mind time for things?

To be clear I don't think there's anything wrong with you wanting me time or decompressing, I just think it might be worth considering: Are you the only one being asked to give up this time during the month of December, or is it equally shared? Because if it is equally shared, I think you should both approach the issue in a way that is about how you two can protect your boundaries and mental health during it; if this is just about you and you aren't thinking of how your partner can get some alone time, you should do that too!

Anyway, I will say that I think the best thing you really can do is TALK to your partner about this. "Hey, I really want some time to myself, I need to decompress and last year was stressful". I don't think there's anything wrong with that, and it is really a problem people don't think about; planning out a lot of holiday events and things but not "you" time; yes, holidays can be hectic and busy and force things into your routine you don't expect, but you also still have to live your life.

Coming Out of the Closet (Literally)

Dear Miss Marcy,

I'm having some serious clutter problems with my hobby. I had a pretty small space in my closet that was devoted to holding boxes and storing things that I was working on, as well as holding my completed models, but the more I get into the hobby, the more space things are taking up, and the closet space I originally had designated is no longer working out. I've considering slimming down and already have some models and stuff I've realized are just never going to happen or work in my army, but honestly, what should I do for storage that isn't just boxes flooding out of my closet?

Storage Wars

Dear Storage,

Ah, yes. A hobby often starts out with one or two items, and suddenly, you've got a tower of things that you have to store, all in various sizes and shapes. Odd how models are a lot easier to store before you build them, huh? Well, then you just have a horde of unbuilt plastic, so then of course you have to build them, but then you have a lot of BUILT plastic, and...

Well, you get the idea.

I think your idea of planning out space was good, but like most hobbyists, we never really seem to plan out the exact RIGHT amount of space we really need. And buying temporary solutions creates long problems, because you'll suddenly find that the thing you did ended up only working for a short period. Your honest best bet is to carve out a serious, specific, and as large as logically possible space that you can. Then, start looking at what types of furniture and storage solutions you can afford in that space. Will it fit a book case? How tall? Wide? Will it allow you to store both unbuilt and built models comfortably? while IKEA is often a very "easy" solution here, it isn't always the best bet. That said, Billy bookcases really do a lot of work for their size, price, and general shape.

The other thing to consider, though, is space, in the empty sense. Something that tends to happen when you make a dedicated space for a hobby is that when you have excess, empty space, your brain tends to start thinking about how you COULD fill it. And, well, that's how we end up with excess models we're suddenly looking to sell. You seem to already be aware of this issue, so just consider that whatever you do end up planning, don't think you need to FILL your space; let it be empty! Trust me!

title: This indie card battler is the kind of board game Kickstarter SHOULD be for
content:
The great promise of crowdfunding was that it would allow people with great ideas but no platform to raise money straight from the public to bring them to life; the reality has been messier, with tiny indie titles competing for space with glossy projects from established publishers using Kickstarter as a pre-order and marketing platform. That makes it a delight to find a project like Scattered Nexus: Solis Wars, an expandable card battler game that its creator has worked on for eight years, and published via the print-on-demand service Game Crafter since 2021. This is a true blue indie, a perfect example of the kind of project that crowdfunding can bring to life.

Scattered Nexus is a head to head card battler with a total of thirty factions, each themed around a different indie comic - the art, graphic design, and rules clarity is very good. Deck construction is similar to Smash-Up: you'll pick three factions and shuffle them together to make a 39 card deck. Your goal is to beat down your opponent with your heroes - hits that connect make them discard cards from their deck, and an empty deck means game over.

There are plenty of complications, special abilities, and event cards as well - the how-to-play video below explains things pretty well. If you want to test it there's even a free online client with a tutorial, basic AI, and the ability to play against your friends online.

There are three main tiers in the Kickstarter: a $5 print and play PDF tier; a $20 physical copy of the latest standalone expansion to the game, Solis War, which comes with six factions; and then a $100 Collectors Box with five previous expansions.

At the time of writing there are still early-bird pledges available for the physical tiers, which knock 25% off those prices. The art and design is all completed, and if the Kickstarter reaches its modest goal of $5,000 that will pay for a print run via established board game manufacturer Magicraft.

This is a genuinely indie operation. Creator Eli Beaird ran the first Kickstarter for a Scattered Nexus set in 2020. It only reached 16% of its funding goal, but Beaird kept on trucking with the project, and by October 2021 he'd listed it on Game Crafter for purchase on a Print on Demand basis. He's released four more expansions since then, and only one of them was paid for by a Kickstarter campaign.

What's your favorite indie gaming find? Is one the best board games in your collection a niche Kickstarter title no-one else has heard of? Is your favorite RPG a zine game you bought from the author at a convention? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Third-party D&D book stars a new class that's half-Warlock, half-Pokémon Trainer
content:
EN World has shared a deep dive into a new D&D class in its upcoming magic-focused Advanced Fifth Edition book, Secrets of the Tome, and in essence it's a Warlock who's incredibly indecisive, or perhaps wants the chance to catch 'em all.

Just like the 5e Warlock class, the Pactweaver gains magical powers by negotiating with powerful entities and spirits, but rather than a permanent pact, their deals are far more fleeting. This makes them highly versatile - with the right preparation they can handle all sorts of different situations.

Secrets of the Tome has over 100 spirits, representing all kinds of things: elements, emotions, animals, ancestors, monsters, the seven deadly sins, and dreams. When a Pactweaver binds one, they add its spells to their spell list and gain other features as well (with stronger spirits there can be negative costs too).

From an outside perspective, this looks to be a way for a player to have a Warlock-like experience but with the flexibility and greater customization of a Wizard. From day to day you can have different spells memorized, based on the situations you're likely to encounter.

EN World provides three examples of spirits of different strengths. A lesser, earth spirit gives three spells (grease, mudhole, slow) and lets you ignore difficult terrain from sticky stuff. A greater, City spirit grants six spells and some street-savvy abilities, and the Arch spirit Mynozua, The Lady of Storms gives you nine spells and lets you zip about and blast people with lightning or send them flying with thunder when you land beside them.

There are also five subclasses launching with this class, some of which focus on summoning particular types of spirits, while others grant you more martial or rogueish abilities.

Secrets of the Tome hits Kickstarter on November 19, 2026. While this is the only brand new class in the book, it also offers seven new subclasses for various casters, including a storyteller bard, snake-oil salesman artificier, and lich-like wizard. Plus there are lots of new spells and magic items.

It's part of Level Up: Advanced 5th Edition, EN Publishing's standalone hack of 5e D&D, which adds lots of new options.

If you're interested in the upcoming book, let us know over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Star Wars Legion: October Painting Challenge
content:
Have you ever complained about not having enough time to paint your models? Do your buddies give you shit for playing with unprimed or unpainted models? Then I have a solution for you: Paintober!

Inspired by the X and 1 Cast (primarily a Star Wars Legion podcast but they also cover Halo Flashpoint on their Orbital Drop Pod(cast)) and their yearly Paintober Challenge, I, Micah (dirtboi), challenged the other Legion contributors to endure the month of pain with me. Or was it painting?

The Rules

31 days, 31 models. Models must be from start to finish within October, either from a built or primed only state, and accompanied by a verification picture when you start. Vehicles still only count as one (thank you Gimli son of Gloin) unless there are separate pilots and riders, which count as their own.

The Prize

"But what if I complete the challenge?" I hear you say. Then you get the best prize of all, bragging rights, and the right to give your friends shit to paint their models. Maybe they need some Paintober in their life!

Mandalorian Sleuth

For my 31 models I went with character models (and cheated). I own all the Star Wars Legion Armies so for me 31 models just means my armies can all share in the painting love.

I don't plan on showing pictures of all of them individually but I do have some I was pretty proud of.

Credit: Mandalorian Sleuth

The list of characters is as follows:

Republic

I decided to go with a beach theme, the only issue I ran into is I don't have any extra sand so currently some minis do not have sand on their base. I also painted the custom Jedi and Yoda jumping in a Dark Side theme for my personal Republic army while the beach theme was for my significant others 332nd Republic Army.

Credit: Mandalorian Sleuth
  • Ashoka (both forms)
  • Yoda (both models)
  • Delta Squad (all 4 minis)
  • Custom Jedi (3)
  • Padme
  • Chewbacca

CIS

I decided to keep with my current CIS theme of Geonosis for their bases.

  • Poggle the Lesser
  • Custom Super Tactical Droid

Rebels

All my rebels are painted and based for Hoth and some I actually used alternate color schemes for. One of my Lukes I decided to paint brown and white instead of the usual black and white.

  • Han Solo (on foot)
  • Princess Leia (Hoth Sculpt)
  • Jyn Erso
  • Luke Skywalker (both forms)
  • Rebel Custom Character (2)

Empire

I decided on a muddy base for these minis, especially with the new 224th Battle Force coming out.

  • Custom Imperial Character (2)

Mercenary

Hondo I went with a base similar to my CIS army but for the Mandalorians I use a concrete looking base to match the ruined Mandalore theme I have for them.

  • Hondo Ohnaka
  • Custom Mandalorian Character (5)
  • Bo Katan with Darksaber

I had a lot of fun with this challenge, but I do look forward to going back and really finishing the detail work on these miniatures. At least my armies have some more painted commanders to lead them into battle. I do consider me cheating to make 31 "character" models by using Delta Squad as 4 of them. Technically any of the Clone Commandos would work for the unit, but I figured this would be a fun time to work on my free handing.

Dirtboi (Micah)

For my 31 models (spoilers, I completed more than 31), I wanted to knock out a huge chunk of my Empire army that has needed some painting love. I have a white board I've started using to keep track of my painting projects (helps the scatter brain) and at the top was 50 Shoretroopers. I have 6 units of Shoretroopers and their respective mortars, 4 from the previous edition that only came in boxes of 7 models, and 2 of the new boxes that include the squad upgrade.

Credit: dirtboi

Throughout my entire Empire army I want an easier paint scheme that my usual oil will carry across the finish line, with a few pop colors and dusty pigment powder bases. I did a heavy white zenital prime over a dark grey prime, then dunked the entire model in Warhammer Skeleton Horde thinned with Contrast Medium and water. Pants and boots were painted over with Warhammer Gore-Grunta Fur, and black capes, eyeslots, and undersuits were Warhammer Black Templar. Blasters were Warhammer Ledbelcher followed by a thinned Black Templar.

For the rank markings, I wanted to follow the screen accurate rank markings found in Rogue One and some scenes of Andor. Unit Leaders and T21B Heavies recived Warhamemr Hoeth Blue markings with a tiny square of Wargammer Flash Gitz Yellow on their Chests. Everyone received a Warhammer Khorne Red right armband, and left (and right on heavies) stripers were Pro Acryl Bold Titanium White with a THIN striped of Warhammer Abbadon Black. Vallejo Desert Sand texture paste for the bases, and plent of Army Painter Jungle, Swamp, and Highland grass tufts to go around.

Bases and grasses

The boys in tan got an oil wash and a hefty dose of Scale 75 Sand Pigment Colors around the base before a black base rim, and glamour shots.

50 Shoretroopers patrolling the beaches. Credit: dirtboi

I had finished all 50 Shoretroopers and gotten a game with them, before it was even the 13th of October. I had technically completed the challenge at this point, but I had so much momentum and it felt really good to complete a chunk of my army, so I kept going.

Credit: dirtboi

Up next, 4 full units of Stormtroopers, 4 units of Scout Troopers, all 4 Imperial High Command, Customizable Officer and Agent, Vader, and the old model of General Veers.

I managed to finish the old PVC model of General Veers in an a few hours, painted and based to match my Imperial Blizzard Force. His uniform was a mix of Army Painter Speedpaint Burnt Moss and Absolution Green, armor was AP Speedpaint Gravelord Grey, boots were Warhammer Black Templar. Two coats of Warhammer Valhallan Blizzard and he is number 51 for Paintober.

Credit: dirtboi

After Veers, I started plugging away on 44 Stormtroopers, General Tagge, and a Customizable Officer and Agent. I just recently played through Star Wars The Force Unleashed, and was super inspired by Triton Squad in the first level. Warhammer Ledbelcher for all the blasters and metal bits, then Warhammer Black Templar for all of the undersuits and over the top of the blasters. Blue striping was Pro Acryl Blue, and I cleaned up some of the paint overspill on the Storms with Pro Acryl Bold Titanium White. Bases are the same as the Shoretroopers mentioned above.

WIP Triton Squad Stormtroopers. Credit: dirtboi

Also at the last minute, decided to paint up 6 Probe Droids, mostly because I'm going to use them in an upcoming event with the Shores and Tagge. Started them with a black prime, drybrushed Ledbelcher, covered them in Black templar, then hit them with a super light drybrush of Warhammer Runefang Steel.

Primed Probe Droids. Credit; dirtboi

For the Officer, I wanted her to be the leader of a Stormtrooper Battalion, so she got an Abaddon Black uniform. For the Agent, I was super-inspired by the ISB Tactical Teams shown off in Andor Season 2. His uniform was the same black as my Officer, and I painted his armor with multiple thin coats of Bold Titanium White. I wanted more color on both of these models, so both of their capes were Khorne Red highlighted with Warhammer Evil Suns Scarlet.

Stormtrooper Battalion Officer WIP. Credit: dirtboi
ISB Agent WIP. Credit: dirtboi

For General Tagge, I couldn't decided on which shade of green for that Imperial Officer green, but I eventually decided on Pro Acryl Camo Green highlighted with Warhammer Straken Green.

ISB Agent WIP. Credit: dirtboi

Hit everything with an oil wash, and my lovely pigment powders, and a black base rim. After the oils, I hit my Officer's droid's eye with some Bolt Titanium White, then some Warhammer Baal Red Contrast, and a little bit of Pro Acryl Fluorescent Red in the center. On the probe droids, I used Pro Acryl Coal Black to clean up the lenses, then used some Warhammer Magos Purple. Went back over the center of the lenses with Pro Acryl Fluorescent Purple, and another coat of Magos Purple. Brushed on the lenses with some AK Interactive Gloss Varnish, and were done!

General Tagge. Credit: dirtboi
Stormtrooper Battalion Officer. Credit: dirtboi
ISB Agent. Credit: dirtboi
6 Imperial Probe Droids. Credit: dirtboi
4 full units of Stormtroopers. Credit: dirtboi

53 more completed for Paintober, making that 104. There is one other model I painted that I'm intentionally leaving off because he's not related to Star Wars Legion.

Credit: dirtboi

Final Thoughts

I am so thrilled that I completed as much as I did. I have never painted with a deadline or challenging myself to get a certain amount of stuff done within said deadline, and it really helped shackle me to my desk to get stuff done as much as possible. Had a lot of fun, and I'm looking forward to next Paintober, and continuing my momentum onto more projects. Huge shoutout to Mandalorian Sleuth for partaking in the pain with me. Tell your friends to get their stuff painted in Paintober!!

title: Warhammer: the Horus Heresy brings back proper Rites of War and end-game scoring in surprise update
content:
On Wednesday, Games Workshop released two free updates to Warhammer: the Horus Heresy which bring back beloved elements of the game that have been missing from third edition. A new set of Legiones Astartes Primary Detachments allows you to build armies laser-focused on a single type of unit - be that elites, jetbikes, tanks, dreadnoughts, or drop assault troops - just like the old Rites of War system; and the updated Core Mission Pack Imperium at War allows end-game scoring once more, just as the Emperor intended.

In the current version of Warhammer: the Horus Heresy, the term 'Rites of War' refers to the unique army rules for each Space Marine Legion, but in previous editions, the term referred to a flexible - if occasionally clunky - system that allowed players to construct army lists that completely rewrote the game's list-building restrictions. These recreated some of the most iconic formations of the Heresy war: the massed Terminator charges of the Justaerin, the armored tank columns of the Iron Hands, or the gravbike cavalry charges of the White Scars.

The new Legiones Astartes Primary Detachments can be taken in place of the standard Crusade Detachment as the core of your army. Each has a unique force organization chart, plus unique restrictions, penalties, and bonuses.

As a quick example, Fury of the Ancients allows you to field 10 War-engines for a massed onslaught of Dreadnoughts. The force can only contain Command and Specialist units that have the Battlesmith (X) special rule; most Auxiliary detachments aren't allowed; and the death of a War-engine grants the opponent an extra VP. It also offers a new Prime Advantage, Ancient of War, which grants a non-malefic War-engine Eternal Warrior (1).

The most radical new Primary Detachment is the Orbital Drop Assault, which makes drop pods meaningful once again. The Drop Assault player takes the second turn by default, but gets to deploy all of their drop pods in a single rain of iron. To diminish the coherency of this assault, you have to roll for each unit on a new Orbital Drop table, which might make them scatter or even get held back in reserves as their flight zone is impeded.

The new Core Mission pack Imperium at War is a vital compliment to the updated Primary Detachments because of one small but incredibly impactful change to mission scoring: vehicles and cavalry can control objective markers. This gives vehicle-only Armoured Spearhead and cavalry-only Sky-Hunter Phalanx armies a fighting chance.

Beyond that, the Imperium at War pack has six deployment maps, three mission categories - holding objectives, slaying enemy units, and holding battlefield sectors - and the option to play missions either with Escalation (progressive) or Hammerblow (end of game) scoring. It's a huge increase over the tiny selection in the core rulebook.

The spirit of the second edition mission War of Lies - in which the actual value of any given objective was only revealed at the end of the game, and could even be negative - lives on in Hidden Caches, which sees every objective marker scatter before it's scored. Cue Yakety Sax as units rush around after vanishing objective markers.

If the sudden inability to run your favorite army list gave you the ick when third edition Horus Heresy launched, are you thinking of going back? I've got a sudden urge to get back to work on my Iron Warriors Fury of the Ancients list… let me know if you're planning to dust off an army in the Wargamer Discord community, and why not share some pics of your legion in our Share Your Army channel?
